en: The Sūtra on the Supernatural Transformations and the Realm of Expedient Means in the Bodhisattva’s Practice,
Volume One,
translated by the Tripitaka Master Guṇabhadra of India during the Song Dynasty.
Thus have I heard:

At one time the Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Ujjayinī, in the park of King Caṇḍaprabha. It was filled with many sāla trees, tāla trees, kaṇikāra trees, nyagrodha trees, plakṣa trees, and udumbara trees;
it was further adorned with vārṣika flowers, dhānīka flowers, atimuktaka flowers, and campaka flowers, as well as aśoka trees and pāṭala trees.
Furthermore, there were springs, wells, ponds, lakes, rivers, and streams of clear water as adornments;
blue, yellow, red, and white lotuses covered all the waters;
and various birds—geese, wild geese, mandarin ducks, *kūṇāla* birds, *pāṭhā-muṇḍa* birds, parrots, mynas, and *jīvajīvaka* birds—uttered diverse sounds.
Many black bees emitted exquisite sounds;
many soft, deep-green grasses spread throughout the great forest.

He was accompanied by a great assembly of twelve hundred million bhikṣus, headed by the venerable Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Mahākāśyapa, Aniruddha, Subhūti, Mahākātyāyana, Mahākapphiṇa, Revata, Pūrṇa, Nandika, Nadīkāśyapa, Gayākāśyapa, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, Gavāmpati, Nanda, Cūḍapanthaka, Ṭaṃbamallaputra, Khadiravanika, Nanda, Mahākauṣṭhila, Rāhula, and the venerable Ānanda.

Twelve billion together entered the practice of the single realm of all phenomena; they entered the practice of the suchness-nature of all dharmas and the practice of space, abiding nowhere and practicing without dependence. Free from all coverings, obstructions, and fetters that arise, they entered the realization of the Tathāgata. There was no dharma-realm near to the one dharma-realm as they proceeded toward the path of omniscience without ceasing. With a mind for omniscience that never regressed, they discerned with wisdom and reached the other shore, diligently cultivating the sphere of skillful means.

Mahāprajāpatī, Yaśodharā, and others, together with eight hundred million bhikṣuṇīs, had all accomplished the pure dharmas and were entirely virtuous in their conduct. Approaching the path of omniscience, they entered the nature of non-existence through their excellent practice; they contemplated all phenomena as being without intrinsic nature or characteristics, and by themselves realized that the reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi) of all dharmas is boundless. Having attained unimpeded wisdom of liberation, they were able to manifest appropriately for the sake of sentient beings according to those who required to be disciplined.
Furthermore, he was accompanied by a great assembly of seventy-two billion bodhisattvas, whose names were: Bodhisattva Great Power,
Bodhisattva Holding Great Power, Bodhisattva Great Transformation, Bodhisattva King of Great Transformation, Bodhisattva Great Advancement,
Bodhisattva Great Advance-Quencher, Bodhisattva Great Roar, and Bodhisattva Great Roaring Mind.
...the Bodhisattva Mahāsanghīśvara, the Bodhisattva Mahāgandhahastin, the Bodhisattva Mahācandra, the Bodhisattva Sucandra,
the Bodhisattva Guṇacandra, the Bodhisattva Ratnacandra, the Bodhisattva Samantaprabhāscandra, the Bodhisattva Dharmavimalacandra,
the Bodhisattva Candraprabha, the Bodhisattva Sujanmacandra, and the Bodhisattva Prabhākarin...
Candraprabha Bodhisattva, Pūrṇacandra Bodhisattva, Brahmaghoṣa Bodhisattva, Brahmasvaranirghoṣa Bodhisattva, Bhūminirghoṣa Bodhisattva,
Dharmadhātunirghoṣa Bodhisattva, Sarvamāramaṇḍalābhibhavanirghoṣa Bodhisattva,
Svaravighuṣṭa Bodhisattva, Samantaghoṣa Bodhisattva, and Nirvikalpavikalpanirghoṣa Bodhisattva.
The Bodhisattvas: Earth-Wheel Sound Bodhisattva, All-Unobstructed Sound Bodhisattva, Universal Treasury Bodhisattva,
Stainless Universal Treasury Bodhisattva, Virtue Treasury Bodhisattva, Illumination Treasury Bodhisattva, Jewel Treasury Bodhisattva,
Moon Treasury Bodhisattva, Sun Treasury Bodhisattva, Blazing Treasury Bodhisattva, and Lotus [Treasury] Bodhisattva.
Bodhisattva Flower Treasury, Bodhisattva Lotus Virtue Treasury, Bodhisattva Great Intention, Bodhisattva Beneficial Intention,
Bodhisattva Wondrous Intention, Bodhisattva Excellent Intention, Bodhisattva Victorious Intention, Bodhisattva Increasing Intention, Bodhisattva Boundless Intention,
Bodhisattva Vast Intention, Bodhisattva Awakened Intention, and Bodhisattva Inexhaustible.
The Bodhisattva Maticandra, the Bodhisattva Sumerupradīpa, the Bodhisattva Mahāpradīpa, the Bodhisattva Dharmolkāpradīpa,
the Bodhisattva Sarvadigavabhāsapradīpa, the Bodhisattva Samantaprabhāsa, the Bodhisattva Sarvatamo’ndhakāravidhamanapradīpa,
the Bodhisattva Sarvamārgāvabhāsapradīpa, the Bodhisattva Ekaprabhāsapradīpa, and the Bodhisattva Candrapradīpa.
Sādhū, the Bodhisattva Sun-Lamp, the Bodhisattva Free from All Evil Paths, the Bodhisattva Unconquered by Māra,
the Bodhisattva Unconquered by Great Māra, the Bodhisattva Majestic Virtue, the Bodhisattva Unconquerable, the Bodhisattva Immeasurable,
the Bodhisattva Majestic Virtue Awakened from Dry Evil, and the Bodhisattva Attained Great Power.
Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, Maitreya Bodhisattva, Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, and others, numbering seventy-two billion, were all in their final birth (*ekajātipratibaddha*);
they had attained *dhāraṇīs*, attained various *samādhis*, attained boundless eloquence (*pratibhāna*), and attained the unimpeded [wisdom] and fearlessnesses. They had obtained...
Having attained supernatural powers (*abhijñā*), they reach the further shore and are able to traverse the boundless buddha-fields.

Wandering through these fields with liberated body and mind, they achieve unimpeded knowledge and vision free from all obstructions. In worlds where no Buddha exists, they manifest the appearance of a Buddha in the world;
they skillfully turn the wheel of Dharma without error, in accordance with the needs of all sentient beings.
Having attained liberation, he preaches the Dharma and the Dharma of non-action; within the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), there is neither movement nor lack of movement.
His mind enters the perfections (*pāramitā*) and reaches the other shore;
he expounds the Dharma of emptiness and lets out the great lion’s roar, subduing and destroying all non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), overcoming Māra and his enemies, and attaining all forms of awakening.
The supernormal powers practiced by the Bodhisattva sever and detach from craving and anger, rendering his mind impartial like earth, water, fire, and wind;
he enters the secret realm of all Tathāgatas and performs the work of a Buddha for the sake of all sentient beings;
he is constantly praised by all Buddhas and upholds all future kalpas.
He upholds the *dharmatā* of all Tathāgatas and rains down the jewels of the Dharma; he extols all his merits, which are inexhaustible.
Having become a sovereign of the world through the fulfillment of his original vows, he practices the conduct of liberation of the Tathāgatas.
Having already skillfully practiced the Mahāyāna in the past, his eye of faith is pure.
Free from defilement, they constantly and diligently provide offerings and service to all Buddhas and Tathāgatas;
they are able to skillfully adorn themselves with the adornment of non-retrogression and advance toward great compassion.
Their minds possess a nature of liberation beyond comparison, transcending doubt regarding the Buddha and the wavering, deluded mind, and they are protected and sustained by the Buddhas of the past.
Furthermore, there were immeasurable upāsakas and upāsikās whose majesty within this trichiliocosm was beyond compare;

as well as devas and lords of devas, nāgas and lords of nāgas, yakṣas and lords of yakṣas, gandharvas and lords of gandharvas, asuras and lords of asuras, garuḍas and lords of garuḍas, mahoragas and lords of mahoragas, kiṃnaras and lords of kiṃnaras, and humans and non-humans and their respective lords—all of whom arrived and sat together with their hundreds of thousands of retinues.

At that time, the World-Honored One, surrounded by a great assembly of immeasurable hundreds of thousands, sat upon the Lion Throne of the Treasury of Virtue; his own radiance was so fierce, brilliant, and stainless that it eclipsed the bodily light of the entire assembly.
Just as Mount Sumeru stands out from the great ocean, eclipsing all other mountains with its radiant and preeminent brilliance;
so too is the World-Honored One, seated upon the lion throne, eclipsing all devas and worldlings, distinguished, powerful, and radiantly pure.
Just as when the moon on the fifteenth day is full, it outshines all the stars with its pure and clear radiance;
so too is the World-Honored One, for he outshines all devas and worldlings with his pure and clear illumination.

Just as the void is clear, pure, and stainless, free from any clouds or mists, and when the sun emits its radiant web of light, it eclipses the glow of mountains and the darkness of fireflies, shining with ultimate brilliance and purity;

so too is the World-Honored One: seated upon the lion throne, he subdues and eclipses all the gods and worldlings, shining with supreme illumination, and likewise eclipsing the radiance of Śakra, Brahmā, and the World-Protectors.
Just as a blazing great fire atop a high mountain illuminates with pure clarity in the darkness of night;
so too is the World-Honored One, seated upon the lion throne, having subdued and eclipsed all devas and worldlings, his radiance supremely illuminating, pure, and stainless.
Just as the lion, king of beasts, subdues all lesser creatures;
so too does the World-Honored One, seated upon the lion throne, subdue and eclipse all devas and humans.
Just as a lapis lazuli wish-fulfilling gem with eight facets is stainless and radiates pure light;
so too is the World-Honored One, seated upon the lion throne, majestic, sublime, and illuminating the ten directions.
Just as a wheel-turning monarch subdues all sentient beings within the four realms;
so too does the World-Honored One, seated upon the lion throne, subdue and overshadow all devas and worldlings.
Just as Śakra Devānām Indra, having donned the Śakrābhilagna-jewel necklace, dwells in the Hall of Good Dharma (Sudharmā) and eclipses the radiance of all other devas;
so too does the World-Honored One, seated upon the lion throne, eclipse and obscure all devas and worldlings, illuminating with pure brilliance.
At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī, having understood the thoughts of the great assembly and beholding the Tathāgata’s body with its magnificent and exalted majesty, reflected thus:
"What is this omen of light? Why is it that as the World-Honored One now sits upon the lion throne, there is such extreme radiance, purity, and extraordinary splendor in this vast assembly?"
"I shall now question the Tathāgata regarding this matter.

At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and with palms joined toward the Buddha, praised him in verse:
"The One of Ten Powers shines with radiant light, Subduing the gods and men of the world."
Equal to that which has no equal in the three realms of existence, there is no being who surpasses him.
Like Sumeru, the abode of the gods, he illuminates all directions;
having subdued and eclipsed all other mountains, he emerges with valor to shine upon the multitude of peaks.
The Buddha’s possession of virtue is likewise so: a mountain of wisdom, he emerges valiantly into the world, subduing all those who are obscured, ever-pure and radiantly illuminating.
Like the moon dwelling in the void, he shines with the merit of both sun and moon.
Filled to the brim and perfectly full, it eclipses all other constellations.
The One of Ten Powers is likewise surrounded by his disciples as stars;
emitting the pure light of the moon, he is able to illuminate the worlds of humans and devas.
Just as the palace of the sun, illuminating and subduing all, so too is the Honored One among Men; he subdues the worlds of humans and devas.
Like a fire upon a mountain peak, he shines through all directions in the darkness of night.
The light of wisdom is thus; the Tamer emits sublime radiance.
Like the lion, king of beasts, who displays his majestic virtue to subdue other animals, so too does he manifest illumination to subdue the hosts of externalists.
The Wheel-Turning King of men, with his majestic power, subdues the world;
The World-Charioteer is likewise, subduing and illuminating all worlds.
The King of the Heaven of the Thirty-three, surpassing all other devas, brings them under his sway.
"The Peerless One is likewise; he subdues and illuminates all multitudes.
At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī, having praised the Buddha with these verses, joined his palms and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"I pray only that the World-Honored One will now, for the sake of this assembly, preach the *Bodhisattvacaryā-pratipatti-upāya-viṣaya-ṛddhi-vikurvāṇa-sūtra*. If sentient beings hear it and aspire toward the supreme practice, they shall give rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
Those who are descending in their practice attain superior progress;
those who have already resolved upon unexcelled bodhicitta increase their scope of the unexcelled bodhi realm;
and indolent sentient beings give rise to great aspiration and joy.
"May sentient beings who have regressed from the Path be established securely on the path to Bodhi;
may all those sentient beings who are proceeding toward the path to Bodhi be fully endowed with the Tathāgata’s perfection of wisdom.
Having thus made this request, Mañjuśrī [fell silent].
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
“What is the cause for which that which is spoken by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha is difficult to understand?
For what cause does he enter [into it]?”

It is difficult to know, difficult to awaken to, difficult to measure, difficult to teach, and difficult to master; those among gods and humans who violate dignified conduct and those who break the precepts cannot understand it;
inferior beings cannot comprehend it;
and those with corrupted minds cannot believe in it.
Those who are under the influence of evil associates cannot enter it;
those who have abandoned virtuous friends cannot know it;

and those who are not protected and sustained by the Buddhas cannot hear or receive it, much less understand and attain it—such a thing is impossible, except for those protected and sustained by the Buddhas.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
“Mañjuśrī, listen to my words regarding the meaning of what you have asked: those who are base and obscured cannot practice it; they do not know this nature of phenomena (dharmatā).”
Those who did not practice under former Buddhas, nor were protected by the World-Honored Tamer;
if they hear this Dharma, they will lack a heart of reverence,
being ensnared by evil associates and separated from those who are virtuous friends.
If they hear such a Dharma as this, they will quickly fall back like a great mountain.
With small minds and no progress, lacking any superior or wondrous resolve, these inferior people have no faith or understanding; such as these do not rejoice upon hearing it.
Out of compassion for them, the Buddha did not speak [of this], lest he should afflict those sentient beings;
because they do not believe in this Dharma, they will find no benefit throughout the long night.
At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

This assembled multitude is entirely pure; they have previously performed virtuous deeds, have extensively made offerings to past Buddhas, have been sustained by spiritual friends, and possess well-purified roots of faith. They revere the supramundane Dharma of liberation, are skilled in purifying the mind, and are ultimately adept at understanding and teaching. Such a multitude as this has gathered together, capable of knowing and understanding a Dharma such as this.”
"Excellent, World-Honored One!
We pray that you will now expound it for the sake of gathering in and benefiting all sentient beings.
He spoke again in verse:
“Many sentient beings here seek the benefit of the Dharma, And skillfully understand and realize this nature of phenomena;
This is what the Buddhas of the past have practiced, Therefore, the Teacher and Subduer proclaims the Dharma.”
All stood with palms joined in reverence, gazing intently at the World’s Tamer;
for their sake, the Tamer conceived a heart of compassion, and the Great Awakened One vowed to proclaim the supreme and wondrous Dharma.
We now all entreat the Dharma King: May you expound the supreme and wondrous Dharma;
For the sake of benefiting and gathering in the bodhisattvas, O Honored One among Men, we pray that you open the treasury of the wholesome Dharma.
After Mañjuśrī had thus made his request, the Buddha praised him, saying: "Excellent, excellent, Mañjuśrī!"
"You have asked the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha about such a matter. Mañjuśrī!
You now fully know the practice of all dharmas; you have no doubts regarding any phenomena, for you have well awakened to wisdom and skillful means."
Mañjuśrī! You have performed many deeds for the benefit of all sentient beings. Mañjuśrī!
"You shall act as a great illumination for all bodhisattvas of the future. Mañjuśrī!
Listen now attentively and reflect upon it well; I shall now speak the *Bodhisattvacaryā-pratipatti-upāya-viṣaya-ṛddhi-vikurvāṇa-sūtra*."
Mañjuśrī and the other bodhisattvas said:
“So be it, World-Honored One!
We shall listen with a sincere mind.”
The Buddha said:
“Good sons! If there are those who accomplish twelve meritorious dharmas, these good sons and good daughters, etc., are able to give rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
What are these twelve?

There is one whose nature of sublime understanding is free from inferior understanding and practice; one whose nature and conduct give rise to compassion born of pure clarity; one whose mind is dedicated to practice, firmly receiving the unconditioned; one who is well-adorned through long cultivation of virtuous deeds; one who is skillfully reverent and makes offerings to all Buddhas, skillfully accumulating pure dharmas; one whose bodily, verbal, and mental actions are non-active and free from all evil; one who stays far from evil associates and draws near to virtuous friends; one who acts according to what they say and says according to what they do, being without flattery or deceit; one who has skillful awakening and knowledge of the Dharma, not craving its flavor, eating with moderation and measure; one who is protected by the Tathāgatas and remains free from the influence of Māra; one who constantly gives rise to a heart of compassion toward all sentient beings, never abandoning them, while the mind itself remains without craving; and one who possesses the power of causes and conditions, adorned with merit.
"Good son! This is called the accomplishment of the twelve dharmas of merit.
Good sons and good daughters who give rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* do so with a beneficial mind, for it is able to bestow happiness upon all sentient beings."
The mind of compassion, because it refrains from committing all evils;
the mind of great pity, because it is capable of bearing the burden of all sentient beings;
the mind of great loving-kindness, because it extinguishes all evil realms.
It is a pure mind, because it does not seek other vehicles;
it is a mind free from attachment, because it is detached from all the turbidity of fetters and afflictions;
it is a purified mind, because its nature is inherently pure.
The mind is like an illusion, for it has no substance;
it is a mind of non-possession, for it is free from possession;
it is a steadfast mind, for it is unshakable.
"The mind of non-retrogression, because it penetrates all dharmas;
the mind that delivers all sentient beings, because it acts according to its word.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"If there are sons of the Buddha who practice well, Whose minds are fulfilled by the pure Dharma,
With hearts of compassion for all sentient beings, And with supple minds directed toward Bodhi."
From the outset, I have distanced myself from evil associates and drawn near to virtuous spiritual friends who point the way to Bodhi;
with a vow to strive diligently for the fruit of Bodhi, I have given rise to the awakening mind of Bodhicitta.
Constantly without a mind of weariness or fatigue, practicing the deeds to be performed as they were at the original limit;
with a non-retrogressive mind like a vajra—one generates the bodhicitta in such ways as these.
With a heart of compassion for all sentient beings, To establish all beings in happiness;
Because they remain far removed from all evils, Such as these quickly give rise to the bodhicitta.
The wise do not seek other vehicles; they contemplate the supreme merits of bodhi.
With a pure mind, free from defilement and craving, such is the desire for the mind of awakening.
Detached from things and compassionate toward things, yet free from attachment; its nature is like lightning, illusions, and the like.
Detached from all things and devoid of characteristics—this is what the Buddha taught as the bodhicitta and so forth.
Free from all latent tendencies and all evils, Stainless and luminous like space,
Wherein no syllables can be perceived— This is called the purity of the bodhicitta.
This is the root of bodhi and the practice of supreme excellence;
it is also the dhāraṇīs and the various eloquences, as well as the faculties and the marks of excellence—these are the merits attained by a Buddha.
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
“When a bodhisattva dwells securely and perceives these twelve merits, they diligently and vigorously practice the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā).”
What are the twelve?
Seeing that the path to enlightenment is peaceful, harmonious, and well-adjusted, one diligently practices the perfection of giving;
seeing great and wealthy clans, one diligently practices the perfection of giving.
Seeing that one is born into a noble and beloved lineage, one diligently practices the perfection of giving;
seeing that one is free from the defilement of stinginess, one diligently practices the perfection of giving;
seeing that the mind of generosity is fully perfected, one diligently practices the perfection of giving.
Seeing that the gates to the realm of hungry ghosts are closed, they diligently practice the perfection of giving;
seeing that abundant wealth is sought after by many and desiring its firm stability, they diligently practice the perfection of giving;
seeing that all necessities are spontaneously and fully provided, they diligently practice the perfection of giving.
Seeing that one must abandon everything through the practice of cultivation, they diligently progress in the practice of the *dānapāramitā*;
seeing that one must relinquish all things by being free from greed and attachment, they diligently progress in the practice of the *dānapāramitā*;
seeing that they shall fulfill the *dānapāramitā*, they diligently progress in the practice of the *dānapāramitā*.

Seeing that one should act with caution according to the Tathāgata’s instructions, they diligently advance in the practice of the dānapāramitā, dedicating all their acts of giving toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
“Good son! This is called the bodhisattva’s seeing these twelve merits and diligently practicing the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā).
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
Seeking peerless omniscience through giving, he relinquishes everything—inner and outer—without sparing his hands, feet, pure eyes, head, bones, or marrow;
thereafter, free from greed or regret, his virtues increase.
May I be born into a noble family as a wondrous prince, Later increase my bodhi and subdue the defilement of greed;
Attaining mastery, may I fulfill the perfection of giving— The generosity praised by all Buddhas.
Seeing with wisdom these benefits of such merit, I shall practice total renunciation.
"Furthermore, sons of good family!
If a bodhisattva perceives these twelve meritorious matters, they will diligently apply themselves with vigor to the practice of the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā)."
What are the twelve?
Seeing that I shall protect, maintain, gather, and accomplish the precepts, I diligently practice the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā);
seeing that I shall advance toward the bodhisattva path, I diligently practice the perfection of ethical discipline.
Seeing that I shall loosen the bonds of the fetters, they diligently practice the perfection of ethical discipline;
seeing that I shall leave all evil realms behind, they diligently practice the perfection of ethical discipline;
seeing that I shall purify all evil realms, they diligently practice the perfection of ethical discipline.
Seeing that I shall achieve non-action of body, speech, and mind, they diligently practice the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā);
seeing that I shall not be censured by the wise, they diligently practice the perfection of ethical discipline;
seeing that I shall cultivate the precepts of heedfulness, they diligently practice the perfection of ethical discipline.
Seeing that I shall bestow fearlessness upon all sentient beings, they diligently practice the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā);
seeing that I shall attain the precepts of body, speech, and mind, they diligently practice the perfection of ethical discipline;
seeing that I shall attain mastery over all phenomena, they diligently practice the perfection of ethical discipline.
Seeing me, one should study the unsurpassed precepts of the Tathāgata and diligently practice the *śīlapāramitā*. Noble son!
This is called the Bodhisattva’s diligent practice of the *śīlapāramitā* because of seeing twelve meritorious matters; this precept is dedicated toward omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"I shall loosen the bonds of the fetters; I shall close the gates to the evil realms.
I shall contemplate sublime and wondrous matters; I shall guard the tail of the cow of precepts."
I shall abide as taught by the Buddha; I shall be praised by the wise;
I shall protect and uphold [the precepts] without ever departing from them; I shall possess the merit of abiding in the precepts;
I shall attain non-action in body and speech; I shall practice non-action in the mind.
I shall well guard my body, speech, and mind; I shall no longer travel upon the evil paths.
If one is heedful, as praised by the Sugata, this is the root of all wholesome karma.
I shall dwell eternally in this place, abandoning all forms of heedlessness;
I shall practice the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), and I shall bring the Buddha-dharma to fulfillment;
I shall purify the precepts of the Tathāgata, for these are the most excellent and unsurpassed of all precepts.
Without hoping for or seeking these merits, if a bodhisattva seeks the supreme path and guards the precepts as a yak protects its tail, they shall obtain all benefits of merit.
"Furthermore, sons of good family!
A bodhisattva practices patience by reflecting upon these thirteen modes of conduct.
What are the thirteen?
One practices patience by realizing that all conditioned phenomena are empty;
one practices patience because no self is to be found;
one practices patience because no sentient being is to be found.
Practicing patience without partiality toward self or others;
practicing patience with ultimate freedom from anger;
and practicing patience by subduing the fetters and latent tendencies.
One practices patience in order to permanently sever greed and hatred;
one practices patience in order to accomplish the primary and secondary marks of a Buddha;
and one practices patience with the desire to be reborn in the Brahma world.
One practices patience by remaining free from the oppression of others;
one practices patience because of the desire to attain the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising;
one practices patience because of the desire to subdue all māras.
Desiring to know and see the immeasurable body of the Tathāgata, one practices patience.
With this patience, one dedicates it entirely toward omniscience. Good son!
"This is called the Bodhisattva seeing thirteen modes of practice while cultivating patience.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"This dharma is empty and non-existent; One seeks for it but finds no sentient being."
Understanding this Dharma, they dwell securely in the merit of patience;
Abandoning both extremes, they harbor no anger toward self or others.
The wise cultivate the power of patience; such is the demonstration of great compassion.
Ultimately free from anger, advancing in the practice of patience without sorrow,
because of awakening to its exhaustion, one cultivates patience that pacifies the fetters;
with marks and signs, form adorned and pure, such a one is born in the Brahma palace.
Firmly advancing with the power of patience, one delights in contemplating auspicious forbearance;
through such great power of patience, the power of Māra is rendered powerless,
and all virtues come to abide therein— therefore, cultivate sublime patience.
"Furthermore, sons of good family!
Bodhisattvas possess twelve adornments for the adornment of their cultivation and progress."
What are the twelve adornments? They are:
the adornment of diligent practice and progress through awakening to all Buddha-dharmas;
and the adornment of diligent practice and progress through visiting the abodes of all Buddhas.
The adornment of diligent application and progress in making offerings to all Tathāgatas;
the adornment of diligent application and progress in teaching and transforming all sentient beings;
and the adornment of diligent application and progress in establishing all sentient beings securely within the Buddha-dharma.
The adornment of diligent practice and progress that extinguishes the ignorance of all sentient beings;
the adornment of diligent practice and progress that bestows the Buddha-wisdom upon all sentient beings;
and the adornment of diligent practice and progress that purifies all buddha-fields.
To cultivate the practices of a bodhisattva without weariness throughout all kalpas until the end of the future, and to diligently cultivate the adornment of vigor;
to diligently cultivate the adornment of vigor so as to reach all Buddha-worlds in the space of a single finger-snap;
and to diligently cultivate the vigor to attain supreme enlightenment and turn the sublime wheel of Dharma in all Buddha-worlds.
“O sons of good family!
This is called the twelfth adornment of the bodhisattva’s diligent practice of exertion.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
“Supreme in courageous effort and free from indolence, these sons of the Buddha advance toward supreme enlightenment;
though they travel to many buddha-fields, they remain ever tireless in their practice.”
To transform sentient beings, they exert firm diligence, Able to endure the mass of suffering for hundreds of thousands of billions of kalpas;
Constantly and eternally striving without indolence, They bestow upon sentient beings the bliss of nirvāṇa.
I vow to cultivate and purify all Buddha-fields, To fully awaken to and know all phenomena;
As the supreme wheel within my worlds, Having turned it, I shall discipline many billions of sentient beings.

In a single thought-moment, the mind awakens to the supreme Bodhi; By dispatching emanations to many lands to subdue beings, The Sons of the Buddha constantly ferry others across to the further shore, Manifesting manifold adornments for the sake of sentient beings.
"Furthermore, sons of good family!
There are twelve modes of practice by which bodhisattvas cultivate meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). What are these twelve?
The practice of burning away the fetters, because they are ultimately not produced;
the practice of dwelling with a rectified mind, because one does not follow after sense objects;
the practice of non-reliance, because one is detached from the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm.
They transcend worldly practices by subduing the concentrations of non-noble ordinary beings;
they increase superior practices by being free from the notion of self;
and they practice sequential meditative absorption by discerning the dhyānas.
The practice of non-existence, because it is free from the perception of existence;
the boundless practice, because it censures the samādhis and dhyānas that have limits;
and the practice of this concentration, because it is perfectly tranquil.
The practice of disciplining the mind, because there is nothing it does not know;
the practice of tranquility, because it guards the sense faculties;

the practice of the sphere of skillful means, because when a bodhisattva cultivates dhyāna, they do not abandon, do not initiate, and do not cultivate through wisdom, pride, views, craving, or recollection.
Therefore, the bodhisattva subdues all those who practice dhyāna.
O sons of good family!
This is called the bodhisattva’s cultivation of meditative concentration through the twelve modes of observation.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"This noble dhyāna-concentration is the practice of those bodhisattvas;
It burns away all fetters and afflictions, so that they never arise again."
Dedicate yourself solely to the cultivation of tranquil meditative concentration (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*), and do not cultivate that which pursues sensory objects.
If there is a mind that does not abide, encourage it to dwell in concentration.
Cultivate the meditation of non-reliance; therein, there is nothing upon which to rely.
Regarding the realms of desire, form, and formlessness, one contemplates them without attachment.
This dhyāna transcends the world; this is what the bodhisattva knows.
Therefore, he subdues all those who abide in non-noble concentrations.
Practicing the successive stages of dhyāna for the sake of attaining mastery,
one therefore relinquishes meditative concentration and returns to birth in the desire realm;
increasing superior and wondrous conduct, the wise cultivate dhyāna.
This is the meditation of the selfless mind, taught for the sake of Bodhisattvas;
it is the practice of immeasurable and boundless conduct, the cultivation of the supreme dhyāna.
Therefore, through this partial dhyāna, one illuminates and brings about subjugation.
Endowed with both wisdom and skillful means, he cultivates dhyāna and possesses great renown;
seeing nothing at all that can be attained, he practices exclusively in pure conduct.
Because he has no basis for reliance, he likewise does not dwell upon any phenomena.
The wise one cultivates dhyāna, relinquishing all signs of phenomena.
Practicing such deeds as these, the wise one cultivates dhyāna;
having attained mastery over the state of a pratyekabuddha, they therefore have no further [deliberate] action.
“O sons of good family!
The bodhisattva enters the perfection of wisdom through twelve modes of practice.
What are these twelve?
The practice of clear comprehension, because it is not obscured by darkness;
the practice of the great torch, because it illuminates all fetters and latent tendencies;
the practice of emitting the net of the light of wisdom, because it is free from ignorance.
The practice of the hook of wisdom, because it uproots the root of ignorance;
the practice of the excellent spear of benefit, because it destroys the net of craving;
the adamantine practice, because it shatters the mountain of fetters.
The practice of the solar palace, because it dries up the mud of stagnation;
the practice of the fire element, because it burns away the trees of birth;
the practice of the mani jewel, because it is free from delusion.
This is the practice of emptiness because there are no entities;
it is the practice of signlessness because there are no signs;
it is the practice of wishlessness because it transcends the three realms.
“Good son! This is called the Bodhisattva’s twelvefold wisdom that enters the Prajñāpāramitā.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"This wisdom surpasses the world; it acts as light to extinguish all darkness.
Like the sun’s torch, it is utterly pure, illuminating the multitude of fetters and proclivities.
Sharp wisdom destroys ignorance; awakening brings about the breaking of craving."
The vajra of the Lord of Devas shatters the mountain of all fetters and afflictions; it destroys all the hosts of asuras.
It attains illumination and leaves darkness behind, manifesting wisdom like a lamp.
Just as the sun dries parched mud, so is transcendent wisdom like the sun;
crossing to the further shore of the ocean of fetters is like a boat crossing water;
uprooting the tree of ignorance is like a sword cutting down all trees.
Having attained the non-delusive maṇi jewel, which is empty and devoid of the nature and characteristics of things;
always free from vitarka and vicāra, and not relying on any path of existence;
having attained the destruction of doubt, one is able to discourse upon and express words.
Revealing the faults and perils of birth and death, Manifesting the torch of nirvāṇa.
This wisdom is the eye that disciplines the world, Appearing as the phenomena of the signless and non-delusive.
Through this wisdom, the bodhisattva is steadfast, Leaving behind darkness to practice the path of enlightenment.
“O sons of noble family!
This Bodhisattva knows and perceives twelve realms of manifested skillful means.
What are these twelve?
"Good son! This bodhisattva reaches the realm of nirvana, yet through skillful means manifests the realm of birth and death;
he reaches the realm of tranquility, yet through skillful means manifests himself amidst the clamor of the multitudes."
Reaching the realm of dhyāna, they employ skillful means to manifest the presence of palace ladies;
reaching the realm of non-action, they employ skillful means to manifest the realm of all conditioned activities;
reaching the realm of non-arising, they employ skillful means to manifest the realm of birth and death.
Having transcended the realm of the four māras, they employ skillful means to manifest the subduing of all māras;
having reached the realm of the sages, they employ skillful means to manifest proximity to the realms of non-sages;
having transcended worldly realms, they employ skillful means to manifest worldly realms.
Having attained the realm of wisdom, they skillfully manifest the realm of ordinary beings;
while clearly perceiving the realm of the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), they skillfully manifest without falling into the realms of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas;
having reached and mastered the signless dharma-realm (*animitta-dharmadhātu*), they skillfully manifest bodies adorned with the primary and secondary marks (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*).
In order to transform sentient beings, they enter the realm of the Buddhas and skillfully manifest the realms of all Māras.
O sons of good family!
This is called the Bodhisattva’s knowledge and vision of the twelve realms and their skillful manifestations.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"This is the realm of skillful means, whereby Bodhisattvas purify sentient beings.
Abiding within this realm, they manifest all realms."
Having attained the realm of nirvāṇa, they employ skillful means to manifest the conditioned;
yet having reached this very realm, they are untainted by the faults of duality.
Having reached the state of tranquility, they employ skillful means to manifest amidst the clamor of the multitude.
Unattached to both, their non-attachment is like that of a bee;
appearing among beautiful women and indulging in the pleasures of the palace,
they attain tranquility— this is the skillful means of those who uphold virtue.
Without retreating from meditative concentration, they manifest a distracted mind through skillful means;
seeing that there are no urgent affairs, they demonstrate through the wisdom of skillful means.
Furthermore, they are without reverence, yet free from false appearances and frivolous discourse.
The realm of non-delusive conceptualization is manifested through the wisdom of skillful means;
neither born nor dying, it is the noble majesty of the unarisen Dharma.
Manifesting within birth and death, the wisdom of skillful means is courageous and steadfast.
Transcending the realm of Māra, they dwell in the realm of majestic Buddhas;
yet they manifest within the realm of Māra—this is the skillful means of the Buddha’s heirs.
Having reached the pinnacle of noble merit, they employ the conduct of ordinary beings as a skillful means.
Sentient beings possess the power of pure wisdom, And through the transformations of skillful means-wisdom, All phenomena are without limit; They know that the primordial limit is empty.
Seeking no personal nirvana— This is sustained by skillful means.
All phenomena are signless; this is the realization that they are empty and non-existent.
Yet, for the sake of transforming sentient beings, they manifest bodies adorned with the marks and signs of excellence.
This is the realm of skillful means, O Son of the Buddha of Great Majestic Virtue!
These sons of the Buddha dwell in peace, manifesting a hundred transformations. "O sons of good family!

You should now know that through the skillful means (*upāya*) of the Tathāgata, twelve meritorious accomplishments are brought forth to refine the buddha-field. Having realized unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment, he manifests the defilement of the eon, the defilement of views, the defilement of sentient beings, the defilement of afflictions, and the defilement of lifespan. He manifests various vehicles; he manifests buddha-fields as foul and impure; he manifests sentient beings as dull-witted; he manifests diverse teachings; he manifests diverse sentient beings; he manifests disputes and contentions among heterodox paths; and he manifests Māras and the deeds of Māra. Yet, in all these there is no fault whatsoever; you should know that all of these are the skillful means of the Tathāgata."
When the Buddha had finished speaking these words, the youth Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

We pray that you will speak of the twelve meritorious qualities that perfect and refine a buddha-field, wherein the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, attain the path of unsurpassed, true, and complete enlightenment.”
The Buddha said, “Mañjuśrī!
This refined buddha-field possesses a refined eon that is fully accomplished and perfected, because it does not abandon the various refined merits.”
It is at this very place that all Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path.
This refined Buddha-field is perfected with refinement because it does not deviate from the timing of the practice of the Dharma.
This refined buddha-field is perfected by the refinement of sentient beings, for there is nothing therein that does not know the Dharma.
This refined buddha-field is perfected by the refinement of the field of merit, for it is virtuous, wondrous, and pure.
This refined buddha-field is fully endowed with refined and easily understood sentient beings, for they are not dull-witted.
This refined buddha-field is fully endowed with the accomplishment of the refined vehicle, for it issues forth from the One Vehicle.
This refined buddha-field is accomplished through a refined and wondrous ground, because it is devoid of material things.
This refined buddha-field is accomplished through a refined and wondrous ground, because all dharmas are practiced without deviation.
This refined buddha-field possesses the accomplishment of refined merit, because it is free from flattery and deceit.
This refined buddha-field possesses the ultimate accomplishment of a refined mind, because it is inhabited by sentient beings of pure nature.
This refined buddha-field is perfected by the presence of refined sages, for its field of merit is not empty.
This refined buddha-field is perfected by the presence of a refined site of enlightenment, for it is the dwelling place of the Buddhas of antiquity.

Mañjuśrī! This is called the Buddha-field perfected and refined by the accomplishment of these twelve merits; it is in this place that all Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, realize the unsurpassed, right, and true path.
Mañjuśrī! You should now know this:
in my realm, there is absolutely no place where śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas dwell.
Why is this? Because the Tathāgata has abandoned all differentiated marks. Mañjuśrī!

If the Tathāgata were to desire the Mahāyāna for some sentient beings while desiring the Hīnayāna for others, then the Tathāgata would possess an impure mind, an unequal mind, the fault of attachment, a partiality of great compassion, and the reproach of discriminatory thought; I, too, would then incur the reproach of being stingy with the Dharma.

Mañjuśrī! If I were to preach the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings, it would all lead toward bodhi, all lead toward the Mahāyāna, enter into omniscience, and result in the attainment of omniscience. For this reason, there is no other vehicle in which one might abide.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If there is no distinct dwelling place for other vehicles, for what reason does the Tathāgata, in his introductory discourse, teach the Dharma to sentient beings by means of the three vehicles, saying: ‘This is the Śrāvaka vehicle; this is the Pratyekabuddha vehicle; this is the Mahāyāna’?”
The Buddha said: “Mañjuśrī!

The vehicle is merely the ground upon which the Tathāgata establishes his dwelling; it is not that the vehicle itself is the dwelling place, nor is it established by means of the characteristics of dharmas. The Tathāgata creates a dwelling place for beings—whether it be a minor adornment or an immeasurable adornment—for that dwelling place is the undifferentiated Dharma-realm, being without distinction.”
Mañjuśrī! The Tathāgata expounds the gate of non-obstruction, proceeding step by step until he reaches his place of abiding. Mañjuśrī!

It is like a craftsman who, having first studied under a skillful master and reached the shore of clever wisdom, employs various expedient means according to what his disciples wish to learn; he causes them to attain clever wisdom by demonstrating various matters of diligent practice—this is the first aspect of clever wisdom.
Mañjuśrī! The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, is likewise so: he is a skillful master of wholesome dharmas and the All-Knowing One, who makes three kinds of teachings. Mañjuśrī!
"Just as a small fire gradually grows until it is capable of burning for an entire kalpa, Mañjuśrī,

so too is this light of omniscience; it increases step by step until it reaches the great wisdom of a Tathāgata, and the radiance of that wisdom burns away all the fetters and afflictions of sentient beings."
“Mañjuśrī! Sumeru, the king of mountains, is free from discrimination; if there are sentient beings who go to its presence, they all become the same color, namely, a single golden color.”
Mañjuśrī! This Sumeru of the unsurpassed great wisdom of the Tathāgata is likewise without any discrimination.
If there are those who contemplate the dharmatā of the Tathāgata, they all see it as having a single color, namely, omniscience.

Mañjuśrī! It is like a great sapphire-colored maṇi jewel; wherever that maṇi jewel resides, within its sphere of influence, there appear rays of light of various colors, namely various hues and various distinct forms.
By the power of the majesty of this maṇi jewel, they all become a single color, namely, blue.
Mañjuśrī, it is the same with the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed deep-blue maṇi jewel: if any sentient beings touch the light of the Tathāgata, they all become a single color—the color of omniscience.

Mañjuśrī! It is like the great ocean: although various streams of water flow into it through manifold gates, once they have entered, they become of a single taste—namely, the salty taste—because it abides eternally.

Mañjuśrī! The great ocean refers to the great wisdom of the Tathāgata. The various waters that enter it refer to all the dharmas of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas; once they have entered, they become of one flavor, because there is no distinction within the One Vehicle.

Mañjuśrī! By this skillful means, you should know that the Tathāgata establishes beings on the ground of falsehood; this is called the Tathāgata’s differentiated guidance and teaching for the sake of providing a place of rest, because it causes them to enter the place of abiding in the Tathāgata’s Dharma, and because the Tathāgata manifests a gradual entry into the Buddha-dharma.

To cause those who possess minor adornments and great adornments to abide in the Buddha-dharma, the Tathāgata, through this skillful means of wisdom and eloquence, manifests various transformations to teach the supramundane; that which is the ultimate truth is the One Vehicle, non-dual.

Mañjuśrī! In this buddha-field, if there are those among the non-Buddhists who practice the life of renunciation, the Tathāgata manifests skillful means therein, protecting and sustaining them with sovereign guidance.
Why is this? Mañjuśrī!
Because the Tathāgata is skillfully able to subdue all enemies and adversaries, the Tathāgata is at all times entirely without enemies or adversaries.
