“Mañjuśrī, it is as if a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin), having accomplished minor merits, possesses a collection of conditioned virtues that are subject to exhaustion; he still has greed, hatred, delusion, grasping, fetters, and latent tendencies. Yet, this wheel-turning monarch has no one at all who acts as his enemy.”
Why is this so? Mañjuśrī! This wheel-turning king is free from contention and affliction.

Mañjuśrī! How much more so for the Tathāgata, who has turned the great wheel of Dharma, who is fully accomplished in the adornment of immeasurable great wisdom and merit, who has attained uninterrupted great compassion, and who traverses the space of the untainted Dharma; having achieved the seven treasures of the factors of enlightenment and turning the great wheel of Dharma through the power of non-forgetfulness, it is impossible that there could be any external disputes, enemies, or fears.
Mañjuśrī, you should know this!
If you see these non-Buddhist renunciants outside of this Buddha-field, you, son of good family, should know that they all abide in a single path, namely, the Buddha-path.
Mañjuśrī! Just as various birds and beasts have no power to remain before the lion king, so it is, Mañjuśrī!

None of those who have left the household life as non-Buddhist outsiders are able to enter the realm of the Tathāgata, nor can they engage in debate with the Tathāgata. It is impossible for anyone to roar in his presence—except by the empowerment of the Tathāgata himself—for he is a Great Being, a Lion who wields the ten powers and has attained the four fearlessnesses.
Mañjuśrī! It is like when the sun’s orb rises and emits a web of light; all fireflies are completely eclipsed, and all precious jewels, fires, and stars lose their illumination.
In this way, Mañjuśrī!

When the Great Sun Tathāgata emerges from his palace, he radiates the light of great wisdom, whereby all those who have left the home life as non-Buddhist outsiders are completely eclipsed and possess no illumination.
Mañjuśrī! It is like a supreme iron king: wherever its territory extends, no other iron can remain there, because the mass of that iron possesses unique characteristics not shared by others.
Thus it is, Mañjuśrī!
If there is a buddha-field where a Buddha has appeared in the world, you should know that none of the various non-Buddhists therein possess the practice of renunciation. Why is this?
Because a Buddha possessing unique characteristics has appeared in the world. Mañjuśrī!
It is like this: wherever the king of wish-fulfilling jewels appears, no counterfeit mani-jewels can arise.
Thus it is, Mañjuśrī! You should know that from this source of the great wisdom-jewel of the Tathāgata, no non-Buddhists (tīrthika) can emerge. Mañjuśrī!
It is, for example, like a place where the nature of jewels produces Jāmbūnada gold; in such a place, inferior metals such as copper do not appear.
In the same way, Mañjuśrī, wherever there is a world in which a Buddha appears, there no heterodox teachers (tīrthika) appear.
Mañjuśrī! You should know that expedient means follow the place where the Buddha appears; it should not appear among those who have gone forth as non-Buddhist outsiders. Mañjuśrī!
You should now know that the Tathāgata maintains an inconceivable realm of skillful means; for this reason, all manner of non-Buddhist renunciants appear within this Buddha-field.

Why is this? Because all the leaders among the various non-Buddhist paths abide in the inconceivable liberation; they emerge from the *prajñāpāramitā* and sport with skillful means, yet they do not abandon mindfulness of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha, teaching and transforming sentient beings until they reach the other shore, for the Tathāgata upholds them as he transforms sentient beings.

When this Dharma was being taught, eight thousand devaputras who relied upon the vehicle of the śrāvakas, upon hearing the teaching of the One Vehicle, gave rise to the mind of unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment;

five hundred bhikṣus attained the Samādhi of the Lamp of the One Vehicle; and one thousand two hundred bodhisattvas attained the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).

This entire trichiliocosm shook in six ways; the devas in the sky rained down blue, yellow, red, and white lotus flowers, and rained down powdered sandalwood. Before the Buddha, hundreds of thousands of devaputras remained in the void, raising their voices in acclamation, while celestial garments whirled of their own accord in the air.
The devas performed music and spoke these words:
“Never before have we heard this sutra appear in the world.
World-Honored One, may this scripture be made to circulate for a long time in Jambudvīpa. Eight hundred bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs then removed their uttarāsaṅga robes and offered them to the Buddha.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"The realm of skillful means is inconceivable; Mañjuśrī, you should know me as such.
When I attained awakening through refinement, I likewise manifested such a time."
I have no fault regarding the passing of time; there is always the opportunity for the sublime Dharma.
Sentient beings cross over through hearing my Dharma; I have no fault regarding the afflictions of sentient beings.
I have refined the remnants of kalpas of meritorious deeds; I have refined the field of merit until it is pure and stainless.
When I attained awakening through such refinement, I therefore know that I am free from turbidity.
For many billions of kalpas past, I have accomplished the immeasurable wisdom of the Buddhas;
as my attainment of the Way was such, so too has been my life, and throughout this interval, there has been no passing into parinirvāṇa.
Through skillful means, I manifest the appearance of parinirvāṇa; because there is the notion of permanence, I manifest impermanence.
I now manifest what remains of my life, for my lifespan is equal to future kalpas.
I have but one vehicle and a single nirvana; A differentiated vehicle cannot be found.
That I speak thus of three vehicles in this way— Know it to be the realm of skillful means.

For those with indolent minds and inferior inclinations, who would feel alarm and fear upon hearing [this], the three vehicles are taught for their sake; yet there is only the One Vehicle, and no second.
I speak according to the inclinations of those who seek the Dharma, so that they may enter the matters of the Buddha-way;
thus, while I expound the One Vehicle as three, there is no impairment to this very vehicle.
Just as one skilled in wisdom reaches the further shore, and by means of that wisdom manifests the three worlds,
so too does the World-Honored One know the supreme Dharma, and by means of this Single Vehicle, expound the three.
With an impartial mind, I guide all sentient beings; I harbor no thoughts of partiality toward them.
If my mind were to take pleasure in or revere the Lesser Vehicle, I would then be guilty of stinginess.
The deep blue lapis lazuli jewel is the most supreme among all jewels;
wherever it may be situated or remain, everything becomes uniformly one color, and that deep blue hue remains without distinction.

The jewel of the wisdom of the Tamer is likewise: it radiates light throughout all buddha-fields, causing all sentient beings to become a single color—the color of the bodhicitta, which is without differentiation.
Just as a small fire, once ignited, gradually grows into a great flame, so too is the flame of a śrāvaka’s wisdom;
it likewise radiates the light of the Buddha’s virtues.

Just as those who turn toward Sumeru, the King of Mountains, become one color through its majestic power, so too is it with taking refuge in the One of Ten Powers: those who possess gentleness and patience attain the color of Bodhi.
Just as the mouths of all bees, Gathering various kinds of pure and wondrous things,
All substances combined together, Produce entirely the single characteristic of honey.

Knowing the world and praising the world is likewise so; having manifested the practice of the three vehicles, and having brought all pure qualities into harmony, one forms the thought of awakening without any other thought.
The Wheel-Turning King of Men is free from sorrow and affliction, for there are no enemies in any other quarter;
since I have issued this universal proclamation throughout the Dharma-realm, how could there be any realm of external paths?
Just as when the solar palace first emerges, it eclipses fireflies and all the stars;
so too does the emergence of the palace of wisdom eclipse the illumination of ignorance of all non-Buddhists.
Wherever superior iron resides, all other iron is unable to move;
likewise, wherever the Tathāgata travels, no followers of external paths can go there.
Wherever gold and jade are produced, no other copper is born in that place;
likewise, in whatever buddha-field one realizes enlightenment, there is no admixture of followers of external paths.
The wish-fulfilling jewel is not mixed with counterfeit jewels; likewise, the past and future are not intermingled.
So too are the Buddha-treasure and the followers of external paths; within a single buddha-field, they are forever unmixed.
With mastery over meditative concentration, supernormal powers, and patience, these non-Buddhists possess the gateway to all-knowledge;
through wisdom, skillful means, and practice, these wise ones manifest various kinds of transformations.
Having heard this regarding the sphere of skillful means, the sons of the Buddha were then filled with great joy;
they experienced a sense of auspicious delight and immeasurable bliss.
They scattered flowers as an offering to the Tamer of Men, and at that moment, the earth shook in six ways, while musical instruments resounded in the sky.
"Billions of devas in the void of space joined their palms and praised, saying, 'Excellent is the teaching of the Tamer!

When this verse was spoken, Satyaka the Nirgrantha, together with eight billion other Nirgranthas, traveled in succession through various kingdoms from the south toward the great city of Ujjayinī, surrounded and adorned by a multitude of hundreds of thousands who cried out and called to one another.

At that time, King Caṇḍapradyota saw from afar the arrival of Saccaka the Nirgrantha. Upon seeing him, he conceived a heart of affection and a heart of pure faith. Together with his great ministers, the ladies of the inner palace, the people of the realm, his children, the fourfold army, and the majesty and supernatural power of a great king—adorned with hundreds of thousands of full jars;
with the sounding of hundreds of thousands of musical instruments and the raising of banners, streamers, and precious parasols as ornaments—he immediately went out to welcome Saccaka the Nirgrantha.
At that time, Saccaka the Nirgrantha saw King Caṇḍapradyota from afar and addressed him with gentle and affectionate words:
"Welcome, Great King!
In your realm, there are no enemies who press you with hostility, nor is there any suffering, affliction, or fever of illness."
"O Great King! Do these ministers, subjects, musicians, soldiers, and wicked, unworthy persons who guard the passes and collect taxes not cause disorder and ruin the kingdom?"
"Are the śramaṇas and brahmins in your kingdom living in peace and happiness?
Great King!
Do you constantly govern the country according to the Dharma?"
"Great King!
You ought not to harm sentient beings by hunting, setting nets, or casting fishing lines to oppress them. Why is this?"
"Great King, you should know that all sentient beings cherish their lives.
Therefore, Great King!"

One should refrain from killing; one should not steal or plunder. One should be content with one’s own royal domain and should not engage in sexual misconduct, being satisfied with one’s own wife. One must never speak falsely but always speak the truth; one should not use double-tongued speech or divisive talk, but should always speak with gentle words; one should not engage in frivolous chatter but should speak according to what is mindful. Furthermore, one should not give rise to covetousness toward the wealth and domains of others.
"Great King!
You should abandon ill will and adorn your body, speech, and mind with loving-kindness.
Great King!"
One should not give rise to wrong views, but practice the noble right view.
Great King!
You must now not be negligent; observe impermanence well.
"Great King, you should know that life is short and fleeting, and one quickly arrives in the next world.
Great King!"
"You should now fear future lives and have faith in the retribution of karma.
He then repeated these excellent verses:
"O Lord of Men, you should always be heedful; be heedful in protecting and upholding your realm."
Those who are heedless fall into evil realms; those who are not heedless are born in good realms.
Do not wrongly take the lives of sentient beings, for all sentient beings cherish their own lives.
A wise person should not harm sentient beings, but should protect them as they would their own bodies.
One should always stay far away from stealing; one should never speak words of falsehood;
one should always uphold truthful speech and vows; Great King, you shall be reborn in a happy realm hereafter.
The speech you utter should be pleasant for the ears to hear; you should not speak with forceful, coarse, or evil words.
You should always speak with love and gentle words; Great King, you should not engage in divisive speech.
Lord of Men, you should not engage in frivolous speech; whatever you say should be spoken in accordance with truth.
Free from the faults and evils of malice, like a great elephant king, you shall be reborn in a happy realm.
O King, you should not engage in sexual misconduct; remain free from desire for the wives and daughters of others, and always be content with the beauty of your own wife.
In this way, you shall be reborn in a happy realm in the future.
Great King, you should not harbor [wrong] views; you should abide securely in the sublime and virtuous view.
You should practice such a Dharma, and thus, Great King, you shall enjoy the pleasures of the celestial realms.
Śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who uphold the precepts, as well as those who are filial and provide for their parents,
having escaped the evil realms, shall receive the joy and bliss of the heavens.

Thus, after the Nirgrantha Saccaka had exhorted King Caṇḍapradyota with this teaching on heedfulness, King Caṇḍapradyota addressed the Nirgrantha Saccaka with words that were affectionate, gentle, and pleasant, saying:
"I shall not do such a thing; you, O Brahmin, may come to my home."
"Why is this? I now invite you and your retinue, desiring to provide you with a meal.
The Nirgrantha replied:
“Excellent, excellent! You should act in this way. Why is that?
"Great King! I have come from afar and am weary and hungry; I require what is necessary. Great King, it is as you have requested.

At that time, the Great King followed behind the retinue of Satyaka Nirgrantha-putra and entered the royal palace. Having entered, Satyaka Nirgrantha sat upon the royal throne, while the other Nirgranthas sat in order according to their rank.
At that time, with a virtuous mind and deep respect, the king personally attended to the needs of the Nirgrantha Saccaka and his retinue until they had eaten their fill.
Then the king thought to himself:
"I shall now briefly question this Nirgrantha Saccaka as to whether he has faith and reverence for the Tathāgata."
Having reflected thus, the king took a small, low seat and sat before the Nirgrantha Sañjayin, saying these words: "Brahmin!..."
"I wish to discuss a few matters; if you grant me leave, I shall question you, and you shall explain them to me.
Saccaka the Nirgrantha said to the Great King:
"Ask whatever you desire as you please; I shall answer well to satisfy your mind."
Having heard and granted permission, the king asked:
"Brahmin! Among the beings in the world, are there any beings who possess wisdom, clarity, and an undisturbed mind, yet nonetheless commit transgressions?"
Saccaka replied, “Indeed there are, Great King!
The king asked again:
“Brāhmaṇa! Who is this? Saccaka replied:
"It was the brahmin Vatsa," [the king] replied.
The king asked again,
"What fault did the brahmin Vatsa commit?"

Saccaka replied: “The Brahmin Vatsa is skilled in observing the stars and calendars, skilled in knowing the seasonal festivals, skilled in the art of chanting and recitation, skilled in knowing lunar eclipses, skilled in knowing earthquakes, skilled in knowing times of plenty and scarcity, skilled in knowing worldly assemblies, and well-trained in physiognomy; yet, in truth, he is an adulterer who covets the wives of others.”
"Great King!
A wise person should not engage in sexual misconduct. Why is this?"
"Great King!
One who commits sexual misconduct will encounter great suffering in both the present life and future lives, and shall even be rebuked by gods and humans.
As it is said in a verse:
"To lust after the wives of others, To fail to guard against evil objects,
And to find no satisfaction in the beauty of one's own wife— These are censured by the world.
The King said:
“Brahmin! Among the beings in the world, are there further beings who possess wisdom that is clear, lucid, and undisturbed in its mental faculty, yet still have faults? Saccaka replied:
"It truly exists, Great King. The king asked, "Who is it?"
Saccaka replied: "This Brāhmaṇa Pāṭikāputra is wise;
he clearly discerns what is the right time and what is not the right time, yet he possesses faults.
The king asked again:
"What fault would there be? He replied, "Great King!"
"This brahmin sleeps excessively, Great King!
A wise person should not sleep too much."
Why is this? Great King!
Through sleep, one falls away from both mundane and supramundane dharmas—whether they be wisdom or abandonment.
As it is said in verse:
"If one delights much in sleep, Enveloped by indolence,
And covered by the negligence of slumber, The ordinary person falls away from all benefits."
The king asked again:
"Brahmin! Among the beings in the world, are there any beings who accomplish such dharmas yet still possess faults?"
Saccaka replied, “Indeed there are, Great King. The king said:
"Who is it? He replied, "Great King, it is Prince Kāla."
The king asked again,
"What fault has this Prince Kṛṣṇa committed? He replied:
"Great King! You are prone to much jealousy.
Great King!"
A wise person should not be excessive in envy.
Why is this? Great King!
If one attains a fiefdom yet acts with jealousy, that person's fiefdom will not be secure; they will die empty-handed, and after death, they will fall into the realm of hungry ghosts.
As it is said in a verse:
"Envy obscures the mind; though such a person may possess a fief, they will die empty-handed and fall into the realm of hungry ghosts."
The King asked again:
"Are there any sentient beings who, having accomplished such superior dharmas of merit, still possess faults and afflictions? Saccaka replied:
"It truly exists, Great King! The king asked, "Who is it?"
He replied, "Great King, it is this Prince Śikhaṇḍin."
The king asked again,
"What fault did Prince Kalyāṇasena commit? They replied:
“Great King! This Prince Śikhaṇḍin takes great delight in taking life.
Great King!”
A wise person should not take pleasure in killing living beings.
Why is this? Killing shortens one's lifespan and leads to rebirth in the hells, as a hungry ghost, or as an animal.
As it is said in verse:
"A king of men who takes life Will have little strength and a short lifespan;
At the end of his life, he will fall into hell. Therefore, do not harm living beings."
The king asked again:
"Brahmin, are there any sentient beings who possess wisdom that is clear and undisturbed, yet whose mental faculty is subject to afflictions? Saccaka replied:
"It truly exists, Great King! The king asked, "Who is it?"
He replied, "Great King, this is none other than Prince Abhaya."
The king asked again,
"What fault did Prince Abhaya commit? They replied:
"Great King! Be deeply compassionate toward others.
Great King!"
A wise person should not feel excessive compassion for others.
Why is this? Great King!
"If one who possesses great compassion for others were to gain sovereign power, this country would be filled with bandits, difficult to subdue, and beset by many calamities.
As it is said in verse:
"If a person who possesses great compassion for others Were to attain sovereign power..."
"One cannot subdue them, nor can one grasp their faults.
The King asked again:
"Among sentient beings, is there any being who is praised by the wise for their wisdom, yet still possesses faults?"
Saccaka replied, “Indeed there are, Great King. The king said:
"Who is it? He replied, "Great King!"
"This Prince Deva-bala is one whose wisdom is praised by the wise,
yet he truly has a fault. The King said, "Brahmin!"
"What fault has Prince Devaśakti committed?
He replied, "Great King!"
Prince Deva-bala drank wine and became dissolute.
O Great King!
A wise person should not drink much wine.
Why is this? Great King!
Excessive alcohol causes the loss of mindfulness, which obstructs the supreme goal, and it also causes the loss of both worldly and world-transcending goals.
As it is said in verse:
"Those who constantly practice heedlessness in all royal affairs, Being shrouded by the intoxication of wine,
are excluded from the meaning of the supramundane."
The king asked again:
"Brahmin! Are there beings who, though praised for their wisdom by the wise, nevertheless possess faults and afflictions?"
Saccaka replied, “Indeed there is, Great King! The king said:
"Who is it? He replied, "Great King!"
"This is Prince Devarāja, who is praised for his wisdom by the wise;
yet he has faults. The king said, "Brahmin!"
"What fault or affliction does Prince Tianxun have?
He replied, "Great King!"
Prince Tianxun, your reflections are excessive.
Great King!
A wise person should not have such excessive reflection.
Why is this? Great King!
Excessive deliberation obstructs and causes loss, preventing weighty matters from arising in tranquility.
Therefore, Great King, one who is truly wise should not engage in prolonged reflection.
As it is said in verse:
"If one harbors excessive deliberation, matters will fail and bring ill fortune;
because of this, one's virtuous adornments will hinder and cause the abandonment of the task of generating the resolve for awakening.
The King asked again:
“Saccaka! Furthermore, are there sentient beings whose wisdom is praised by the wise, yet who still possess faults and afflictions? Saccaka replied:
"It truly exists, Great King! The king said, "Who is it?"
He replied: "Great King!
This is Prince Mahāsena; he is praised for his wisdom by the wise, yet he possesses certain faults."
The king asked again,
"What fault did Prince Mahāsena commit? They replied:
“Great King! There is the fault of being obscured by great stinginess and evil, which plunders the wealth of others.
Great King!”
"The wise should not harbor great stinginess or evil.
As it is said in a verse:
"If a lord of men possesses stinginess, he will receive his fiefdom yet remain insatiable."
"This accumulated wealth will lead to sorrow in the next world.
The king asked again: "Satyaka!"
"Furthermore, there is that which is praised by the wise as wisdom,
yet possesses faults and afflictions? Saccaka replied, "Indeed there is, Great King!"
The king asked, "Who is it? He replied:
"Great King! King Prasenajit is praised by the wise for his wisdom, yet he still possesses faults.
The king said:
“Brahmin! What faults or calamities does King Prasenajit have? He replied:
“Great King! King Prasenajit has the fault of eating too much.
Great King!”
Now, one who possesses wisdom should not eat excessively.
Why is this? Great King!
"If one eats too much, the body becomes weary and heavy, and what has been consumed is difficult to digest.
As it is said in verse:
"O Lord of Men, eating too much leads to weariness and heaviness of the body, and furthermore, it impairs one's discernment."
"His appearance is not radiant.
The King asked again: "Brahmin!..."
"Among the sentient beings of the world, there are those who possess wisdom and are praised for their wisdom,
yet they still have faults and afflictions? Saccaka replied, "Indeed there are, Great King!"
The king asked, "Who is it? He replied:
“Great King! You are indeed one whose wisdom is praised by the wise in this world; yet you too have faults.”
The king said:
"Brahmin! What fault have I committed?"
He replied: "Great King!
You are excessively violent and cruel, of a wicked nature, impulsive and coarse, and devoid of compassion."
"O Great King!

One who possesses wisdom should not be coarse or violent. If a wise person is coarse and violent, people will not flock to them in great numbers; even their own parents will find it displeasing, let alone other sentient beings."
"O Great King!
A wise person should not be coarse or violent.
O Great King!"
"A person of wisdom should reflect deeply and long.
As it is said in verse:
"If one is coarse and violent, and does not cultivate wakeful reflection, there will surely be reproach."
"No one will attach themselves to him.
At that time, King Caṇḍapradyota, hearing of his own faults directly, was filled with anger, resentment, and vexation; his mind was ill at ease, and he could not endure it.
He said to the Nirgrantha Saccaka,
"Should you not rather reproach me here in this great assembly?
Out of anger, he then ordered that he be executed.
At that time, Satyaka was struck with alarm and fear, and spoke these words to the king: "Great King!
You should not act so rashly; grant me fearlessness and listen to what I have to say."
The king said, “I grant you fearlessness; what do you wish to say?
“Great King! [he replied.]

I too have erred; in the presence of my king, I spoke of the king’s faults and evils, saying that he was excessively tyrannical, of a wicked and impulsive nature, coarse and cruel, and devoid of compassion—I spoke these things according to reality.
"O Great King!
A wise person should not speak of another's actual faults at all times.
O Great King!"
A wise person should know the proper time and the improper time.
Why is this so, Great King?
"To speak of others as they truly are often causes displeasure; people do not draw near to such a person, and those lacking wisdom will revile them.
As it is said in verse:
"When one speaks of a king according to reality, The ordinary worldling will disparage him."
"Therefore, the wise, after careful reflection, speak.
At that time, the king praised him, saying, "Well said! and asked again: "Brahmin!..."
"Among the sentient beings in the world, are there any who possess clear wisdom, whose minds are undisturbed,
and who are free from fault? Saccaka replied,
"Indeed there are, Great King!"
The king asked, "Who is it? They replied:
"Great King! This śramaṇa Gautama is of the Śākya royal lineage, having gone forth from among the Śākyas; as we observe him, he is without fault."
Because his lineage is noble, he is without fault; because he is born into the clan of a universal monarch (cakravartin), he is without fault;
because he is not born into a lowly caste, he is without fault.
Because he was born into the Śākya clan, there is no fault.
Because his physical appearance and majestic virtue are exceedingly sublime, there is no fault.
Because he is adorned with the primary and secondary marks of excellence, there is no fault.
For this reason, there is no fault.
This Śākyamuni Gautama, had he not left the household life, would have become a great Wheel-Turning King (Cakravartin), endowed with the seven treasures:

namely, the wheel treasure, the elephant treasure, the horse treasure, the mani-jewel treasure, the woman treasure, the householder-treasure, and the military commander treasure. He would have been possessed of a thousand sons, all valiant, heroic, and handsome, capable of defeating enemy hosts, and each endowed with the marks of a Wheel-Turning King, exercising sovereign rule over the four continents.
The King of the True Dharma does not employ weapons, but governs the nation through the True Dharma.
Having already left the household life, he practiced asceticism for six years, eating only one sesame seed and one grain of rice each day, and sat beneath the Bodhi tree to subdue the hosts of Māra.

Having thus subdued them, with the wisdom of a single thought-moment, he perceives all things exactly as they are known, as they are attained, as they are touched, as they are realized, and as they are realized through direct experience; among all sentient beings, there is none equal to him, let alone any who are superior.
This Śramaṇa Gautama has no equal; therefore, he is without fault.
Why is this so, Great King?

This śramaṇa Gautama is of peerless noble lineage; in physical beauty and majestic virtue there is no one equal to him, and in wisdom and majestic virtue there is no one equal to him; therefore, he is faultless.
As it is said in verse:
“Bearing the thirty-two marks of excellence, Born into the Śākya clan as a lion among men,
The crown prince of King Śuddhodana, The World-Honored One, the Omniscient One, free from all fault.”
When Saccaka the Nirgrantha had spoken thus, King Pāyāsi said: "Great Brahmin!
You should now explain: what are the thirty-two marks of a great man belonging to the Tathāgata?"
The brahmin said, "I shall now speak. The king said:
"What do you mean? "Great King!

This śramaṇa Gautama stands with a firm and stable posture; the soles of his feet are level and full, marked with wheels whose spokes are complete; his hands and feet are soft and supple; his fingers and toes are long and slender, and his hands and feet are joined by webbing."
This śramaṇa Gautama has heels that are full and level, and his foot bones are linked like a chain.
This śramaṇa Gautama has calves like those of an antelope.
This śramaṇa Gautama is upright and handsome in body.
This śramaṇa Gautama has the male organ concealed within a sheath.
This śramaṇa Gautama has body hairs that grow one by one, curling to the right.
This śramaṇa Gautama has body hairs that all point upward.
This śramaṇa Gautama has hair of deep blue-black.
This śramaṇa Gautama has skin that is golden in color, exceedingly fine and soft.
This śramaṇa Gautama is perfected in seven parts.
This śramaṇa Gautama has a body that is well-proportioned and full.
This śramaṇa Gautama has extremely beautiful limbs and joints. This śramaṇa Gautama...
His body is not crooked.
This Śramaṇa Gautama’s body is exceedingly tall and broad.
This Śramaṇa Gautama’s entire body is perfectly rounded like a nyagrodha tree.
This śramaṇa Gautama has a body like that of a lion king.
This śramaṇa Gautama possesses forty teeth.
This śramaṇa Gautama’s teeth are closely set.
This śramaṇa Gautama has even teeth; this śramaṇa Gautama has bright white teeth;
this śramaṇa Gautama possesses the supreme sense of taste.
This śramaṇa Gautama has a broad and long tongue.
This śramaṇa Gautama possesses the Brahma-voice.
This śramaṇa Gautama blinks both eyes simultaneously.
This śramaṇa Gautama has eyes that are deep blue.
This śramaṇa Gautama is endowed with the mark of the white tuft of hair between the eyebrows.
This śramaṇa Gautama has a crown-protrusion upon his head.
"Great King!
This śramaṇa Gautama is endowed with the thirty-two marks of a great man; for this reason, he is without fault.
As it is said in a verse:
"Born into the Śākya clan with a crown-protrusion upon his head, his hair is deep blue and curls to the right;
his eyes are like blue lotuses, blinking like those of a bull-king—for this reason, the World-Honored One is without fault."
With a voice like that of the kalaviṅka bird and pure as Brahmā’s, His tongue is long, broad, clean, fresh, and thin;
Among men, the World-Honored One’s teeth are even and closely set, Forty teeth in all, white and pure.
All people of the world and the various devas, Beholding this beauty, are filled with joy.
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, has a tongue that completely covers his face; therefore, no sentient being is his equal.
All various flavors are gathered together and transformed into a single flavor by the mark of the World-Honored One’s tongue; thus, the World-Honored One is free from all fault.
With a body like that of a lion and lips like the *bimba* fruit, his shoulders are majestic, broad, and well-filled;
the World-Honored One’s body is like the *nyagrodha* tree, perfectly rounded and well-proportioned.
The World-Honored One’s adorned body is upright and straight; the body of this Lion among Men is exceedingly long and broad.
The seven places are rounded and full, peerless in comparison; his exquisite golden hue is most excellent, fresh, and pure.
The hair of this Lion among Men flows upward; his body and skin are exceedingly fine and soft, and each lock of his topknot is formed like a spiral shell; therefore, no sentient being is his equal.
Furthermore, his lion-like stance is neither bent nor drooping; his private parts are concealed like those of a stallion king;
his thighs are rounded and full, and his calves are like those of the deer-king—whom would not bring joy upon beholding him?
The World-Honored One’s hands and feet possess webbed membranes; his fingers are slender and long with copper-colored nails.
His heels are full and even, his ankle bones are hidden like a chain, and the soles of his feet are level and complete, without any unevenness.
The World-Honored One’s hands and feet are adorned and supple; his slender, long fingers are all marked with wheels.
The feet of the Honored One among Men are stable and level; when he walks upon the earth, they do not wobble.
With such marks as none can equal, the Lamp of the World is thus beautifully adorned;
standing amidst the great assembly, he is most venerable and sublime, like the Moon King among the stars.
Such is the physical form of this Great Man; the World-Honored One acts as a lamp for the world.
How much more so regarding the other outflow-free dharmas—by means of these dharmas, he has attained spontaneous awakening.
“Great King! This śramaṇa Gautama possesses a most noble and wondrous complexion; among all sentient beings, there is none who can equal him. For this reason, he is without fault.”
"Great King!

This śramaṇa Gautama has perfected the power of great compassion; his mind is unimpeded toward all sentient beings. He constantly practices great compassion that is unobstructed and unattached, spontaneously reaching all worlds and entering among all sentient beings."
"Great King!
Just as a maṇi jewel can purify turbid water—because the nature of the jewel is pure, it is able to make all turbid water clear and pure.
Great King!"
The śramaṇa Gautama is likewise; because he is pure within, he is able to purify the turbid mud of the fetters and afflictions of all sentient beings, and for this reason, he is without fault.
As it is said in verse:
"May a mind of loving-kindness pervade the world, All worlds throughout the three periods of time;
The minds of all sentient beings— May the Omniscient One extend universal compassion."
There is nowhere it does not reach universally; this loving-kindness has no equal.
It covers the realm of empty space everywhere; no one surpasses the All-Knowing One.
Like a well-purified maṇi jewel, it can purify turbid water.
The World-Honored One purifies all realms of existence and cleanses the defilements of the fetters of sentient beings.
"Great King! This śramaṇa Gautama has accomplished thirty-two practices of great compassion."
What are these thirty-two?
Seeing that the sentient beings of the world are submerged in the darkness of ignorance, this śramaṇa Gautama practices great compassion toward these sentient beings.
Seeing that sentient beings in the world are within the shell of great ignorance, this śramaṇa Gautama exercises great compassion toward these sentient beings.
Seeing that sentient beings in the world have fallen into the great cycle of birth and death, this śramaṇa Gautama exercises great compassion toward these sentient beings.
Seeing that the beings of the world constantly and diligently practice unwholesome and quiescent dharmas, the śramaṇa Gautama gives rise to great compassion for these beings.
Seeing that the beings of the world follow the great current and flow along with it, the śramaṇa Gautama gives rise to great compassion for these beings.
Seeing the beings of the world fallen into the great mountains of suffering and oppressed by intense pain, the śramaṇa Gautama gives rise to great compassion for these beings.
Seeing the beings of the world departed from the noble path and fallen into false paths, the śramaṇa Gautama gives rise to great compassion for these beings.
Seeing the sentient beings of the world confined in a great prison and naturally bound by its shackles, this śramaṇa Gautama conceives great compassion for these sentient beings.

Seeing the sentient beings of the world greedily attached to forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles, never finding satisfaction nor fulfillment therein, this śramaṇa Gautama conceives great compassion for these sentient beings.
Seeing that the sentient beings of the world are slaves to craving and are perpetually bound to others, the śramaṇa Gautama arouses great compassion for these sentient beings.
Seeing that the sentient beings of the world are oppressed by old age and death, weakened, and exhausted, the śramaṇa Gautama arouses great compassion for these sentient beings.
Seeing that the sentient beings of the world are constantly oppressed by illness, this śramaṇa Gautama gives rise to great compassion for these sentient beings.
Seeing that the sentient beings of the world are constantly scorched and consumed by the burning of the three fires, this śramaṇa Gautama gives rise to great compassion for these sentient beings.
Seeing that the beings of the world are bound by lower fetters and increase their cycle of birth and death, the śramaṇa Gautama arouses great compassion for these beings.
Seeing that the minds of the beings of the world are constantly filled with alarm and fear, the śramaṇa Gautama arouses great compassion for these beings.
Seeing that the beings of the world crave meager pleasures and fail to perceive their dangers, the śramaṇa Gautama conceives great compassion for these beings.
Seeing that the beings of the world have long been asleep in negligence, the śramaṇa Gautama conceives great compassion for these beings.
Seeing that sentient beings in the world have fallen into great famine and constantly harm one another, this śramaṇa Gautama conceives great compassion for these sentient beings.
Seeing that sentient beings in the world are constantly in a state of decline and perpetually plunder one another, this śramaṇa Gautama conceives great compassion for these sentient beings.
Seeing that the sentient beings of the world are blinded by ignorance and are perpetually lacking clarity, this śramaṇa Gautama gives rise to great compassion for these sentient beings.

Seeing that the sentient beings of the world are constantly engaged in mutual strife and contention, never ceasing their turmoil, this śramaṇa Gautama gives rise to great compassion for these sentient beings.
Seeing the beings of the world like overgrown weeds and thistles, this śramaṇa Gautama gives rise to great compassion for these beings.
Seeing the beings of the world engage in impure union and remain far from purity, this śramaṇa Gautama gives rise to great compassion for these beings.
Seeing that the beings of the world engage in various hardships while remaining far from the absence of hardship, this śramaṇa Gautama gives rise to great compassion for these beings.
Seeing that the beings of the world are largely beset by doubt and attachment to false views, this śramaṇa Gautama gives rise to great compassion for these beings.
Seeing the beings of the world as being like cotton flowers dependent upon various views, the śramaṇa Gautama conceives great compassion for these beings.

Seeing that the beings of the world possess inversions of perception, mind, and view—conceiving the impermanent to be permanent, suffering to be happiness, the impure to be pure, and non-self to be self—the śramaṇa Gautama conceives great compassion for these beings.
Seeing the beings of the world carrying heavy burdens and constantly suffering from exhaustion, this śramaṇa Gautama gives rise to great compassion for these beings.
Seeing the beings of the world relying on frail, inferior, and unstable conceptions, this śramaṇa Gautama gives rise to great compassion for these beings.
Seeing that sentient beings in the world are constantly defiled, the śramaṇa Gautama gives rise to great compassion for these sentient beings.
Seeing that sentient beings in the world are bound by desire and existence and their minds are greedily attached, the śramaṇa Gautama gives rise to great compassion for these sentient beings.
Seeing that the beings of the world are shrouded by gain and offerings and constantly seek after profit, the śramaṇa Gautama conceives great compassion for these beings.

Seeing that the beings of the world have fallen into various sufferings of illness, lamentation, weeping, and distress—a great mass of manifold suffering—the śramaṇa Gautama conceives great compassion for these beings.
"Great King!
Because this śramaṇa Gautama has accomplished these thirty-two kinds of great compassionate practices, he is therefore without fault.
As it is said in verse:

“Ignorance is a great, dark gloom of delusion; seeing sentient beings shrouded by the shell of ignorance, and seeing sentient beings wandering toward the prison of birth and death, the Honored One among Men thus gives rise to great compassion.”
Sentient beings constantly and diligently perform various deeds; The Perfectly Awakened One sees them drifting and wandering in the stream.
Always following along with this drifting and wandering, The One of Ten Powers constantly gives rise to great compassion.
Falling from the highest and greatest mountain, seeing sentient beings wandering on false paths,
he establishes them securely upon the noble path, dwelling in peace and tranquility, free from affliction.
Bound by various wrong views, unsatisfied in the realms of craving and anger,
and submerged by birth, old age, and death— for this reason, the One of Ten Powers possesses great compassion.

Oppressed by manifold sufferings, seeing the three fires of the world burning fiercely, he was struck with alarm and fear and donned the deer skin; for this reason, the One of Ten Powers feels compassion.
Sentient beings are greedily attached to flavors and indulgent in their attachment to sensory objects;
seeing them fallen into the path of hunger, the Tamer is able to rescue them from harm.
Seeing all sentient beings harming one another, Enshrouded by the darkness of ignorance,
Like the spreading vines and stalks of thorny grass, For this reason, the One of Ten Powers feels compassion.

Bound by the fetters born of sensual desire, seeing sentient beings performing difficult deeds and wandering through the dense forest of wrong views— for these reasons, the One of Ten Powers feels compassion.
Perceiving purity within the impure, permanence within the impermanent, and a self within the non-self;
seeing all sentient beings weary of their heavy burden—for these reasons, the One of Ten Powers gives rise to compassion.
Seeing them burdened by a heavy load, ordinary beings constantly relying on what is weak and inferior,
and perpetually defiled by the various fetters— for this reason, the One of Ten Powers possesses great compassion.

Seeing those who are shrouded by gain and offerings, and furthermore, those who are never satiated with sensory objects and have fallen into the great ocean of the realm of desire— for these reasons, the One of Ten Powers possesses great compassion.
Abounding in various sorrows and ailments, having seen all sentient beings in such distress,
for the sake of all these sufferings and afflictions, the One of Ten Powers possesses great compassion.
Knowing that which is neither existent nor non-existent, he always possesses a heart of great compassion;
with a mind that pervades all sentient beings, he is therefore the All-Knowing One without fault.

"Great King! To speak briefly once more: this śramaṇa Gautama has accomplished the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the four dhyānas, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path."
He is endowed with all perfections; therefore, Great King, this śramaṇa Gautama is without fault.
As it is said in a verse:
"Always diligently cultivating the foundations of mindfulness, the Great Awakened One is well-versed in the right exertions;
the Great Sage has attained mastery over meditative concentration, excelling all beings without fault."
The Tamer of the World has perfected all supernormal powers; with mastery over all eloquence, he has reached the further shore.
The Tathāgata well understands the spells of liberation; the Great Awakened One has thoroughly penetrated all truths.
Having attained mastery in the holy life, practicing loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity,
and dwelling securely in concentration and wisdom, one is therefore forever free from all faults and transgressions.
The Great Sage well knows the aids to enlightenment; The Tathāgata well knows the Noble Eightfold Path.
Seeing sentient beings suffering upon the Noble Path, He brings them to rest ultimately on the shore of peace and bliss.
In all worlds there are no sentient beings who are equal to the World-Regulator;
having attained omniscience and perfected all virtues, he never disparages others.
“Great King! This śramaṇa Gautama has accomplished the ten powers.
The king said:
“Great Brahmin! What are these called the ten powers of the Tathāgata? “Great King!”
This Buddha-Tathāgata knows, as they truly are, what is possible and what is impossible;
he knows, as they truly are, the actions performed and the results received in the past, future, and present, as well as the causes and retributions of their abodes;
and he knows, as they truly are, the immeasurable realms and the various worlds.
He knows, as they truly are, the various understandings of other persons and other sentient beings;
he knows, as they truly are, the faculties of other sentient beings and other persons, whether superior or non-superior;
and he knows, as they truly are, all paths leading to their respective destinations.

He knows, as they truly are, the various faculties and powers of other sentient beings and other persons, as well as their factors conducive to enlightenment, dhyānas, liberations, concentrations, and successive attainments; he knows, as they truly are, all their fetters—whether defiled or pure—and their respective states.
He recollects his immeasurable and manifold past lives, whether one birth or immeasurable births, knowing them as they truly were in terms of their conduct and their speech.

With the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, he sees sentient beings passing away and being reborn in various ways, even up to their birth in good or evil destinies, knowing them as they truly are.
He knows, as it truly is, the destruction of all taints, the liberation of mind through the absence of taints, and the liberation by wisdom. Great King,
this is called the Tathāgata’s accomplishment of the ten powers.
"Because he is endowed with power, he is called the 'Possessor of the Ten Powers' (Daśabala) and is called 'Unconquerable'; therefore, he is without fault.
As it is said in verse:
"He knows, as they truly are, what is possible and what is impossible;"
He is without fault; he is unobstructed in the past. He possesses wisdom regarding the future and the present, and knows that nothing shall be lost.
He well understands karmic retribution and knows that there are causes and conditions; he knows things as they truly are without error—the World-Charioteer knows this.
He knows the immeasurable and manifold realms; being well-versed in all realms, he is peerless among the people of the world.
The various understandings of the world—immeasurable Buddhas, who illuminate the world with clear knowledge, perceive them as they truly are, without error.
They know those of dull faculties, and they know those of middling faculties; they also know those of mature faculties who have reached the further shore.
He knows all paths leading everywhere as they truly are;
he understands individually the faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment, supernormal knowledges, liberations, defilements, and purities.
Free from all obstructions, his knowledge and vision are unimpeded; mindful of equality, he is immeasurable and accords with reality.
Regarding himself and others, he perceives them as they truly are, without distinction.
With the purified divine eye, surpassing that of human eyes, he sees all beings in birth and death;
as a Tamer of Men, he perceives them all.
He knows the exhaustion of all outflows and likewise knows liberation; he fully knows and sees both the state without outflows and its distinctions.
This is the power of the Honored One, awakened and sovereign; it exists within a single thought, yet the mind is free from discrimination.
Its movement is not an act of initiating, for it exists spontaneously; when first turning the wheel of Dharma, there is no practice of discrimination.
With a single mind, he knows the thoughts and the minds of all sentient beings; they possess no dual characteristics.
Therefore, being free from fault, the Buddha attains mastery, and from him all wholesome dharmas and all virtuous qualities emerge.
“Great King! This śramaṇa Gautama has accomplished the four fearlessnesses.
The king asked again:
“Great Brahmin! What are the four fearlessnesses of the Tathāgata? “Great King!”
This śramaṇa Gautama declares of himself:
"I have attained perfect and complete enlightenment.
Yet, there may be śramaṇas, brahmins, Māras, Brahmās, or anyone else in the world who says:

"You lack correct and universal knowledge regarding all phenomena; I do not perceive such a characteristic in you. Because I do not perceive such a characteristic, I abide in peace and I abide without fear."
He declared: "I have attained the practice of the most supreme state; amidst the great assembly, I roar the true lion’s roar and am able to turn the Brahma-wheel.
Among śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and all other worldly beings, there is none who can turn this wheel of the True Dharma."
The Buddha himself made this vow:
"I have exhausted all outflows. If anyone should say:
"Your outflows are not yet exhausted.

Because the Buddha does not perceive such signs, and because he does not perceive signs, the Tathāgata attains the practice of peace and bliss, attains the practice of fearlessness, and attains the practice of the supreme state; amidst the great assembly, he rightly roars the lion's roar and is able to turn the Brahma-wheel.
"Among śramaṇas, brahmins, and all others in the world, there is no one capable of overturning this True Dharma.
The Buddha has taught the dharmas that obstruct the Path.
If anyone were to say:"
"By drawing near to this Dharma, there is no obstruction.
The Buddha does not perceive such signs; because he does not perceive signs, he attains the practice of peaceful bliss, the practice of fearlessness, and the practice of the supreme state.
In the midst of the great assembly, he truly roars the lion’s roar and turns the Brahma-wheel.
Among śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and all others in the world, there is none who is able to turn this wheel of the True Dharma.
I speak of the noble path leading out [of suffering]. If anyone were to say,
"One who associates with this cannot transcend the world," [they would be speaking falsely].

The Buddha does not perceive these signs; because he does not perceive them, he attains the practice of peace and bliss, the practice of fearlessness, and the practice of the supreme state. Amidst the great assembly, he rightly roars the lion’s roar and is able to turn the Brahma-wheel.
"O Great King! Among śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and all other beings in the world, there is none who can turn back this true wheel of Dharma.

This is the Tathāgata’s four kinds of fearlessness; having accomplished these four fearlessnesses, the Tathāgata rightly roars the lion's roar amidst the great assembly, and for this reason, he is without fault."
As it is said in a verse:
"Roaring the lion’s roar amidst the assembly, The Tamer of Men is fearless;
There is none equal to me, Much less any being who has transgressed."
If the Dharma realized by me is true and not false,
and is the vision of the Perfectly Awakened One, then let this be the lion’s roar of the Deer King.
If there be anyone who contradicts it, may they find no such sign [of truth].
Because I do not perceive signs, I am disciplined and fearless.
All my outflows are exhausted; my body is free from outflows.
There is no one equal to me among the gods or the people of the world.
There are these obstructive dharmas, as taught by the World’s Tamer;
they are truly empty and void, and there is nothing that can alter them.
I have proclaimed the dharma of the path to liberation, having realized it myself and now expounding it.
For one who practices this Dharma, there shall be no obstacles.
Having realized this, the Great Hero, the Tathāgata, attained peace and happiness;
he attained the bliss of fearlessness, the supreme conduct of a Great Man.
He turns the Brahma-wheel, which none other is able to turn;
that which is not turned by anyone else in the world, save for the Honored One among Two-Legged Beings.
