"Furthermore, Great King!
This śramaṇa Gautama has accomplished the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (āveṇika-buddhadharma).
Great King!"
What are the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha? Great King! This Buddha, the Tathāgata, has no errors;

his speech is never in vain; he has no loss of mindfulness; he has no divergent thoughts; he has no unconcentrated mind; there is nothing he does not know. His relinquishment of desire does not diminish; his vigor does not diminish; his mindfulness does not diminish; his wisdom does not diminish; his liberation does not diminish; and his knowledge and vision of liberation also do not diminish. All his bodily actions are preceded by wisdom and follow after wisdom; all his verbal actions are preceded by wisdom and follow after wisdom; all his mental actions are preceded by wisdom and follow after wisdom. He possesses unimpeded knowledge and vision regarding the past; he possesses unimpeded knowledge and vision regarding the future; and he possesses unimpeded knowledge and vision regarding the present.
"Great King!
This is called the accomplishment of the eighteen unique qualities of a Tathāgata; therefore, there is no fault.
As it is said in verse:
“The World-Honored One is free from delusion; his speech is without idle talk;
his mindfulness never falters; therefore he is without fault.
He has no divergent thoughts; with right knowledge, his mind is undisturbed.”
At all times he does not give rise to equanimity; his omniscience is without fault.
His desire never diminishes, and his excellent vows never wane in vigor;
his mindfulness is without loss, and no one can destroy it.
Wisdom is without loss or decline; understanding is without decline;
in understanding, knowledge, and vision there is no decrease, and that wisdom is free from affliction.
All bodily actions, as well as verbal and mental actions—
Through mastery over the power of wisdom, that wisdom is never lost.
Knowing the past, that wisdom is without obstruction;
it is unobstructed regarding the future and unobstructed regarding the present world.
"Such are his merits; he is the śramaṇa Gautama.
Yet they exceed these by the immeasurable, such that my speech could never fully exhaust them.
At that time, King Caṇḍapradyota, having heard of these inconceivable merits of the Tathāgata, was deeply satisfied in his mind; he leaped for joy and gave rise to affection and delight.

Thereupon, in the presence of Satyaka Nirgranthaputra, he attained immeasurable joy; he conceived the thought of the inconceivable, the thought of the World-Honored One, the thought of a virtuous friend, the thought of one who reveals Bodhi, the thought of one who has crossed over to that state of omniscience, the thought of one to be entreated for instruction, the thought of mindfulness, and further, the thought of the inconceivable liberation of a bodhisattva.
Having attained such thoughts and states of mind, he then offered a pearl necklace worth hundreds of thousands [of gold pieces], as well as priceless garments, in worship to Satyaka Nirgranthaputra.
Thus he praised him, saying:
"Excellent, excellent! Saccaka the Nirgrantha, you have well explained the Dharma of the sequential skillful means."
He further said: "Satyaka! The Dharma you have preached accords with all-knowledge;

the Dharma you have preached reaches all-knowledge; the Dharma you have preached emerges from birth and death; the Dharma you have preached extinguishes the defilements of the fetters; the Dharma you have preached shatters the gate of envy; the Dharma you have preached beats the great drum of giving; the Dharma you have preached can destroy Māra’s great mountain of arrogance; the Dharma you have preached can dry up the ocean of craving; the Dharma you have preached illuminates the forest of ignorance; and the Dharma you have preached teaches and transforms sentient beings without missing the proper time."
When the king had spoken thus, Saccaka the Nirgrantha said to the Great King: “It is so, Great King!

There is no conduct of a bodhisattva that does not discipline sentient beings; there is no teaching of the Dharma that contradicts the Mahāyāna. It is impossible that it should fail to increase all-knowledge, fail to exhaust all fetters and afflictions, fail to demonstrate the faults and perils of saṃsāra, fail to reach nirvāṇa, fail to approach the practice of a bodhisattva, or fail to attain self-benefit, benefit for others, and the benefit of both.”
"Great King!
If there is anyone who, at the very moment they first resolve their mind [for enlightenment], immediately attains the benefit of self, the benefit of others, and the benefit of both.
When Saccaka the Nirgrantha spoke these words, King Caṇḍapradyota attained the faith that cuts through doubt and attained indestructible faith.
The sixteen princes attained the realm of joyful faith and practice;
eight thousand devaputras obtained the samādhi named "Adornment of the Buddha’s Conduct.

Within the royal palace, there were thirteen thousand *nirgranthas* seated there who conceived the aspiration for unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment. Each of them removed their robes to offer as an act of worship to the *nirgrantha* Satyaka, and then spoke these words:
"We have now obtained a great benefit in that we have seen this great son of good family, Satyaka, and have heard him expound this Dharma that accords with reality.
They spoke further, saying: "Satyaka!..."
"You may go together with me, for you wish to see the World-Honored One; this Buddha, the Tathāgata, is now in my garden.
Satyaka replied, "Let everyone come together in harmony and go."
At that time, the Great King, together with his retinue, ministers, and people, made grand preparations. Then the Great King issued a proclamation throughout the city, saying:
"If anyone does not go to the presence of the Tathāgata, they shall be executed."

Upon hearing the king’s command, all the men, women, boys, and girls throughout the city each took up flower garlands, ointments, powdered incense, and various musical instruments; they departed from the great city of Ujjayinī and waited for the Great King at the edge of the park.

At that time, King Pāṭaliputra, together with the Nirgrantha Saccaka, his various ministers, princes, military hosts, ladies of the inner palace, and the people of the realm, was surrounded by a retinue of mounted attendants. With the majesty of a great king, the great supernatural power of a king, the great transformations of a king, and the great displays of a king, they held aloft banners, pennants, and parasols; there were hundreds of thousands of musical instruments, songs, dances, and performances, as flutes, pipes, and rhythmic clapping produced all manner of exquisite sounds.

Elephants and horses performed acrobatic feats, and hundreds of thousands of auspicious jars marched in the vanguard. Adorned with golden chains, elephant-chariots and horse-chariots followed, surrounded by a multitude of ninety-eight billion people, as they proceeded toward their own park to visit the World-Honored One.
Having arrived, they prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and withdrew to stand to one side.

Saccaka the Nirgrantha and his retinue, having prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and circumambulated him countless hundreds of thousands of times to the right, stood with palms joined, gazing at the Buddha without blinking.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra saw the Nirgrantha Saccaka gazing at the Buddha before him with eyes that did not blink for a moment; having seen this, he reflected:
"For what reason has the Nirgrantha Saccaka come here?"
Having reflected thus, he said to the Nirgrantha Saccaka: "Saccaka!
For what reason have you come to the presence of the Tathāgata? Is it because you wish to see the Tathāgata, or do you wish to listen to the Dharma?"
Saccaka the Nirgrantha replied: "Venerable Śāriputra!
I have neither seen the Buddha nor come to hear the Dharma."
"Venerable Śāriputra!
It is not for the sake of any dharma that I have now gone to the place of the Tathāgata. Why is this?"
"Venerable Śāriputra!
To see form is not called seeing the Tathāgata; to see feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness is likewise not called seeing the Tathāgata."

Not seeing the great elements of earth, water, fire, and wind is called seeing the Tathāgata; not seeing a self is called seeing the Tathāgata; not seeing sentient beings, not seeing a life-span, and not seeing a nourisher is called seeing the Tathāgata; not seeing a person is called seeing the Tathāgata; not seeing "I am superior" or "what belongs to me is superior" is called seeing the Tathāgata; and not seeing conceptualization is called seeing the Tathāgata.

"Venerable Śāriputra! One who does not perceive any marks is said to see the Tathāgata; one who does not perceive attachment is said to see the Tathāgata; seeing that there are no entities is called seeing the Tathāgata; seeing intrinsic nature is called seeing the Tathāgata; seeing the primordial limit is called seeing the Tathāgata; seeing the eye and forms as free from desire is called seeing the Tathāgata; seeing the ear and sounds as signless is called seeing the Tathāgata; seeing the nose and odors as non-conjoined is called seeing the Tathāgata; seeing the tongue and tastes as nameless is called seeing the Tathāgata; seeing the body and tangibles as without sensation is called seeing the Tathāgata; and seeing the mind and phenomena as without discrimination is called seeing the Tathāgata."
Śāriputra said: “Satyaka! If one sees the Tathāgata by means of such characteristics, how does one see the Tathāgata?”
Saccaka replied: "Venerable Śāriputra! One does not see the Tathāgata by way of lineage, nor does one see the Tathāgata by way of nature.

It is neither with marks nor without marks; neither a dharma nor a non-dharma; neither real nor unreal; neither a sphere of experience nor a non-sphere of experience; neither thought nor non-thought; neither conceptualization nor non-conceptualization; neither conditioned nor unconditioned; neither a thing nor a non-thing; neither an aggregation nor a dispersion; and it is neither form, nor sensation, nor perception, nor mental formations, nor consciousness; neither grasping nor non-grasping—this is called seeing the Tathāgata."
Śāriputra said: “Satyaka! Since you see the Tathāgata by means of such characteristics, how, O virtuous man, do you perceive the Tathāgata?”
Saccaka replied: "Venerable Śāriputra!
I do not see the Tathāgata by reaching form, nor do I see the Tathāgata by departing from form, nor do I see the Tathāgata by destroying form."

In this same way, regarding feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness: one does not see the Tathāgata by reaching consciousness, nor does one see the Tathāgata by departing from consciousness, nor does one see the Tathāgata by destroying consciousness.
I do not see the Tathāgata by way of the present portion, nor do I see the Tathāgata by way of the past portion;
I do not see the Tathāgata by way of the aggregates (*skandha*), nor do I see the Tathāgata by way of the elements (*dhātu*);
it is in this manner that I see the Tathāgata.

To see that all verbal expressions are non-expressions is called seeing the Tathāgata. I neither see nor do not see; I am neither existent nor non-existent; I neither discriminate nor do not discriminate;

I am neither thought-construction, nor contention, nor affliction, nor arising, nor grasping, nor abandoning, nor conceptual proliferation; I neither form conceptions nor do not form conceptions; I neither create things nor do not create things; I neither initiate movement nor do not initiate movement; I neither form views nor have no views; I neither perceive objects nor do not perceive objects; I neither speak nor do not speak—to thus see is to see the Tathāgata.
To be free from all speech, discourse, and sound is called seeing the Tathāgata; yet, there is nothing seen.
Venerable Śāriputra!
"A Bodhisattva perceives the Tathāgata in this way, and I likewise perceive the Tathāgata in this way.
Śāriputra said: "If you perceive the Tathāgata in this way, how then do you hear the preaching of the Dharma?"
Saccaka replied: "Venerable Śāriputra!
If I were to listen to the Tathāgata preaching the Dharma, and if a perception of dharmas were to arise in me, that would not be the perception of dharmas."
Why is this? Venerable Śāriputra!
All the speech of a bodhisattva issues forth from the Dharma, yet they do not cling to it, nor do they give rise to conceptual notions regarding it.
"Why is this? Because they are free from the notion of dharmas. Śāriputra said:
“Saccaka, do you not seek to hear the Dharma by approaching the Tathāgata?
Saccaka replied, “Venerable Śāriputra! ”
"Did I not come to the Tathāgata neither seeking the Dharma nor not seeking the Dharma?
For what reason, Venerable Śāriputra?"
Now, one who seeks the Dharma does not seek it within any phenomena whatsoever. Venerable Śāriputra!

One who seeks the Dharma does not seek by clinging to the Buddha, does not seek by clinging to the Dharma, and does not seek by clinging to the Saṅgha. They do not seek by knowing suffering, nor seek by abandoning its origin, nor seek by cultivating the path, nor seek by realizing cessation. They do not seek by transcending the desire realm, nor seek by transcending the form realm or the formless realm. They do not seek within saṃsāra, nor do they seek within nirvāṇa.
"Venerable Śāriputra!
You should know that I have come to the presence of the Tathāgata because I do not seek anything at all among all dharmas. Śāriputra said:
"For what reason do you speak thus?
Saccaka replied, "Venerable Śāriputra!"
I teach that all phenomena are without causes and conditions.
Furthermore, as for the nature of the dharma-realm, it neither possesses causes and conditions nor is it devoid of causes and conditions, for both are unapprehendable.
Śāriputra asked, "Are you now wandering through the various realms of existence? Satyaka replied:
"Venerable Śāriputra! If there were a path, I would undergo transmigration; if there were birth, I would have birth; if there were going, I would have death."
"Venerable Śāriputra!
All dharmas have neither going nor birth-and-death. Śāriputra said:
“Satyaka! As the Buddha has said, ‘You bhikṣus are subject to birth, old age, sickness, and death. Satyaka replied:
“Venerable Śāriputra! Because all sentient beings rely upon the path of existence and arrogance, the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One,
has spoken thus in order to destroy such reliance:”
"The Buddha-dharma is like the true nature; it is devoid of such things as birth, old age, sickness, and death.
Śāriputra said, "Excellent, excellent!"
“Satyaka! You have explained the meaning of discerning the Mahāyāna. Satyaka replied:
"Venerable Śāriputra!
Are you now able to know what this meaning is,
and how it is to be distinguished?"
Śāriputra said: "Good son! I am not the speaker; I now wish to listen."
"Good son! You should explain this: what is the meaning of this, and how is it to be distinguished?"
Saccaka replied: "Venerable Śāriputra!
'Meaning' refers to that which is beyond verbal expression; if there is verbal expression, it is called conceptual discrimination."
Furthermore, "meaning" refers to that which is ineffable; if there is verbal expression, it is called conceptual differentiation (*vikalpa*).
Furthermore, "meaning" refers to silence; if there is verbal expression, it is called conceptual differentiation.

Furthermore, as for its meaning: it is without fluctuation and free from all conceptual proliferation; it is without discrimination and without adornment; it is neither existent nor a thing, and is devoid of the notion of a self.
It is not courageous; it cannot be grasped and cannot be seen; it has no abiding place, being free from all talk of abiding places.
Furthermore, "discrimination" refers to deliberation, calculation, and contemplation that extends to the minds of others.
Furthermore, "meaning" refers to the analytical knowledge of meaning (*arthapratibhāna*).

"Discrimination" refers to the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*), the analytical knowledge of expression (*niruktipratisaṃvid*), and the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhānapratisaṃvid*). Venerable Śāriputra!
"This is called the brief explanation of the meaning and its analysis.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised Saccaka the Nirgrantha:
"Excellent, excellent!"
"Good son! It is as you have said.

When this Dharma was spoken, three thousand devaputras attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti), and twenty thousand sentient beings, hearing this great eloquence, gave rise to the mind of unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi-citta).
At that time, the Venerable Maudgalyāyana addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
How many sentient beings has this good man Satyaka transformed by wearing the garb of these non-Buddhist Nirgranthas?"
The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana:
"If all devas and humans were to hear this matter, they would all become bewildered, with the sole exception of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas."

Maudgalyāyana, listen attentively; I shall now describe a small portion of the various forms, garments, complexions, and deportments of Satyaka the Nirgrantha, as well as his activities in teaching and transforming sentient beings.
Maudgalyāyana!

This son of good family, Satyaka, wearing the garb of a non-Buddhist ascetic, has taught and transformed as many sentient beings as there are atoms in Mount Sumeru, causing them to resolve upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path to enlightenment.

Assuming the form and attire of a Cakravartin, he transformed as many sentient beings as there are motes of dust in the four continents, causing them to resolve upon the unsurpassed, true, and correct path to enlightenment.

Assuming the appearance of renunciants from other heterodox paths, he transformed eighty-four *gaṅgā*-sands of sentient beings, causing them to resolve upon the unsurpassed, true, and correct path to enlightenment.
Manifesting in the form of a śrāvaka, they transform sentient beings equal in number to the sands of ten Ganges Rivers;
having shown them the Śrāvaka Vehicle, they subsequently further transform them, causing them to resolve upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path to enlightenment.
Manifesting in the form of a pratyekabuddha, he transforms and guides sentient beings in numbers even greater than this.
Manifesting in the form and attire of a bodhisattva, he transforms and guides sentient beings in numbers even greater than this.

He further manifested the form of Śakra, the form of Brahmā, the form of a great universal monarch (cakravartin), the form of a world-protector (lokapāla), the form of a kiṃnara, the form of an asura, the form of a garuḍa, the form of a mahoraga, the form of a human, and the form of a non-human; he further manifested the form of a man, the form of a woman, the form of a boy, and the form of a girl; he further manifested the form of the Earth Deity (Pṛthivīdevatā), the form of a spontaneously born deva, the form of a rishi, the form of a young brahmin, the form of a bhikṣu, the form of a bhikṣuṇī, the form of an upāsaka, and the form of an upāsikā.
"Maudgalyāyana!
The young man Satyaka has thus taught and transformed a vast number of sentient beings.
At that time, Maudgalyāyana addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How many Tathāgatas has this Sañjayin Nirgrantha served and made offerings to?
The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana:

"Even if one were able to measure the limits of empty space, there is no one who can reach the limit of the son of good family Satyaka’s various forms of offerings and service to the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas."
Maudgalyāyana!

Even if one were able to reach the limits of the earth element, the water element, the fire element, the wind element, and the realm of sentient beings, there is no one who can reach the limit of this son of good family, Satyaka, who has served and made offerings to the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas.
At that time, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa said to the young man Satyaka, "Young man!
You have served and made offerings to many Buddhas; your merit is fully perfected. For what reason do you not attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path?"
Saccaka replied: "Venerable Kāśyapa!
If there were any enlightenment, or anyone who could awaken to enlightenment, then I would awaken to the unsurpassed right path."
The Venerable Kāśyapa said to Satyaka:
"Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges have made the vow for bodhi; they have awakened to, are awakening to, and will awaken to the unsurpassed, right, and true path."
Saccaka replied: "Venerable Kāśyapa, such a calculation is made for the sake of conceited beings; in the ultimate sense, there is no bodhi, nor is there anyone who awakens to bodhi."
Why is this? Venerable Kāśyapa!
Bodhi is unconditioned and transcends all numerical categories; bodhi is not form, for it cannot be seen.
Awakening is not blue, not yellow, not red, not white, not purple, and not crystal-colored; it has no form or image, no appearance, and no marks, transcending all marks;
it has no dwelling place, having severed all dwelling places;
it is not existent, being free from all existence.
It is without marks, being free from all marks; it is beyond verbal expression, for it is not within the reach of vocal karma;

it is neither a view, nor an accumulation, nor a substantial entity; it is neither darkness nor light, formless and without substance; it cannot be described, yet is not indescribable; it is neither tangible, nor cognizable, nor audible, nor sound, nor a sentence; it is neither bound, nor fettered, nor liberated, nor defiled; it is neither hatred, nor delusion, nor any worldly affair; it is neither a provisional designation nor a non-provisional designation.
Venerable Kāśyapa! Such is the nature of bodhi.
Furthermore, bodhi is not something realized by the body.
Furthermore, awakening is not something realized by the mind.
Why is this? Venerable Kāśyapa!
The body is deluded and devoid of wisdom, like grass, wood, walls, or clods of earth; therefore, it cannot awaken.
That which is the bodhicitta is not form and is moreover invisible;
thus, it likewise cannot awaken to bodhi, nor is there any sentient being who can awaken to bodhi.
Venerable Kāśyapa!
The nature of all dharmas is entirely like this. Why do you say:
"Why do you not attain the unsurpassed, right path?
At that time, the Bodhisattva, the great assembly of Śrāvakas, the upāsakas and upāsikās, as well as Śakra, Brahmā, and the World-Protectors, thought thus:
"O World-Honored One!..."

Knowing the minds of sentient beings as they truly are, according to what you understand, the Tathāgata should sever our doubts and hesitations; please grant the prophecy for the son of good family, Satyaka, as to when he shall attain the unsurpassed, right path.
What shall this world be named?
After attaining bodhi, what shall your title be?
And for how long will you abide in this life?
“How large is this great assembly?
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in the minds of the bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, upāsakas, upāsikās, Śakra, Brahmā, and the world-protectors, addressed Mañjuśrī:

“This good man Satyaka, after this Bhadrakalpa has passed, and after further kalpas beyond calculation have elapsed, shall become a Buddha named Sārthavāhābhimukharāja Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha. That Buddha’s world shall be named Sudarśanasaṃbhava, and the kalpa shall be named Kṣiptakaṇṭaka.”

Mañjuśrī! This world-system, Well-Contemplated Renown, is exquisite and most delightful; it is adorned all around with hundreds of thousands of the seven treasures, and its perimeter is embellished by walls made of the seven treasures. There are hundreds of thousands of moats, filled therein with the seven kinds of fragrant water.
Furthermore, there were hundreds of thousands of lofty and grand towers and pavilions, composed of the seven kinds of great jewels, including lapis lazuli.
They were adorned with hundreds of thousands of millions of Jāmbūnada gold nets that completely covered them.
There were hundreds of thousands of millions of mani-jewels interspersed upon the terraces; there were hundreds of thousands of millions of *siṃha* (lion) mani-jewels adorning the windows and eaves;
there were hundreds of thousands of millions of *siṃhadhvaja* (lion-banner) mani-jewels adorning the precious thrones;
and there were hundreds of thousands of millions of great banner mani-jewels, illuminating all things.
A hundred thousand million nets of bells produced harmonious, soft, and exquisite sounds that filled the entire space.
A hundred thousand million jeweled golden nets were suspended, and a hundred thousand million kinds of banners with various signs were erected.

Mañjuśrī! In this world-system called Well-Viewed Renown, the ground is as level as the palm of a hand and is completely covered by jewel trees that grow soft grass. This grass curls to the right, possessing the color of the neck of a *nandivardhana* peacock, and its touch is like celestial raiment; this grass pervades the entire world-system of Well-Viewed Renown.
There are hundreds of thousands of millions of gardens serving as adornments; each individual garden, in turn, is surrounded and adorned by hundreds of thousands of millions of gardens.
There are hundreds of thousands of millions of ponds adorning the surroundings everywhere, and each of these ponds is interspersed with eight-sided *maṇi* jewels.

It has stairways made of Jambūnada gold, with its floor strewn with golden sand and filled with water of eight virtues; precious flowers are spread everywhere, and geese, wild ducks, and mandarin ducks warble in harmony.

Mañjuśrī! In the world-system called Well-Contemplated Renown, hundreds of thousands of myriads of lands, cities, towns, and villages are universally adorned. Within each of these great cities, there are again hundreds of thousands of myriads of cities surrounding them in adornment; the various villages, towns, and hamlets are likewise so.
All these lands, cities, towns, and villages are filled with men and women.

Mañjuśrī! Within this world-system called Well-Contemplated Renown, there is a four-continent world named Immediately Seen, which is exceedingly extraordinary, most wonderfully sublime, and extremely prosperous and joyful. It is filled with many men and women, and therein the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Real-Intention-Aspect King shall be born.
Mañjuśrī! This Tathāgata King of True Intention was born of the Brahmin caste; his mother’s name was Vīryavatī, just as my mother’s name is Māyā;
his father’s name was Brahmāpraśasta, just as my royal father’s name is Śuddhodana.
He shall have a son named Viśvānara, just as my son is now named Rāhula;
he shall have a queen named Mahāmati, just as my wife is now the Śākya maiden Gopikā;
and he shall have a wet-nurse named Mahāyaśas, just as my wet-nurse was Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī.
That Buddha, the World-Honored One, shall have an attendant named Constantly Following Practice (Sadānuvartana), just as my attendant is named Channa;

that Tathāgata shall have a great horse-king named Great Power (Mahābala), whom King Real Intention (Satyasaṃjñaka) shall mount when he leaves the home life, just as my horse-king today is named Kanthaka;

that Tathāgata shall have a place of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) named Dharma Courage (Dharmavīra), and upon that site, that Tathāgata shall attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path, surrounded by eight billion bodhi trees as adornments.
Mañjuśrī! At that time, those Buddhas had no Māras and no hosts of Māra-devas. Mañjuśrī!

In that future age, when King Śuddhāśaya becomes a Tathāgata, a Samyaksaṃbuddha, all sentient beings in that Buddha-world will produce various musical performances, using every kind of flower, incense, garland, and manifold instrumental music.

We should go together to the Dharma-Vīra bodhimaṇḍa; from the Akaniṣṭha heaven above, all the assemblies shall gather, including the hosts of nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas—all shall assemble—and the great bodhisattvas from the east, west, south, and north shall all assemble there.

Mañjuśrī! After this King of True Intention had first awakened to bodhi, he preached this *Bodhisattvacaryā-pratipatti-vidhi-gocara-abhijñā-vikurvaṇa-sūtra* amidst a great assembly, surrounded by immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of other sūtras.
Mañjuśrī! When that Tathāgata King of True Intention preached this sutra, sentient beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges attained non-retrogression from anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Mañjuśrī! This Tathāgata King of True Intention does not preach the Dharma of the Three Vehicles; in that Buddha-world, there are no śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, for only sentient beings with the wondrous understanding of the Single Vehicle are born in that world.

Mañjuśrī! At the first assembly when that Tathāgata, the World-Honored One King of True Intention, preaches the Dharma, there shall be bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges who attain non-retrogression.
At the second great assembly, eighty nayutas of bodhisattvas shall attain the stage of being born only once more before enlightenment.
At the third great assembly, there shall be sixty vibharas of bodhisattvas.
From this time forward, there shall be bodhisattvas beyond calculation who will dwell securely in the non-retrogressive path to unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment. Mañjuśrī!
Once that Buddha, King of the Mark of True Intention, has attained the Way, his lifespan shall be sixty intermediate kalpas.

After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the True Dharma shall remain in the world for eighty billion hundred thousand nayutas of years; the relics of the Buddha shall be widely disseminated, and the number of sentient beings he will convert shall be equal to that of his previous lives.
Mañjuśrī! When that Buddha was about to enter parinirvāṇa, he bestowed the prediction of enlightenment upon the Bodhisattva Mahālakṣaṇa and only then passed away.
This Bodhisattva Mahālakṣaṇa shall, after me, attain unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment, and be known by the name Tathāgata Mahāvyūha, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
At that time, this great assembly felt doubt and wonder in their hearts:

"Who was that Bodhisattva Mahālakṣaṇa at that time, who, following that World-Honored One, was destined to attain the unsurpassed, true, and correct path, and be named the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Mahāvyūha?"
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts of the great assembly, addressed the youth Mañjuśrī:

"This young boy among the non-Buddhist outsiders sitting before us is named Satyananda; he has surpassed all other youths. He shall attain Buddhahood under the name Mahāvyūha Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha. The adornments of that Buddha’s world shall be no different from those of the Tathāgata Satyasaṃdhikarāja."

When this assembly heard of the majestic power and the adornments of merit of that buddha-field, sixty billion hundred thousand nayutas of bodhisattvas within the gathering resolved to be born in that buddha-world and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."
"When this King of True Intention attains Buddhahood, we shall be born in that Buddha-world.
The World-Honored One then granted the prediction that they would indeed be born in that land.
There were eight billion Nirgranthas who, with one voice, cried out:
"World-Honored One!
We, too, shall be born in that Buddha-land."
The Buddha granted the prediction that all would be born in that land.
Then, from the sky above, ninety billion hundred thousand nayutas of devaputras spoke these words:
“World-Honored One!
When that Buddha, King of True Intentional Marks, attains enlightenment, we shall be born within that world called Well-Contemplated Renown and shall behold such adornments of merit.
The Buddha then gave this prediction:
"You sons of heaven shall also be born in that realm called *Sudarśanābhidhāna* to serve that Buddha.
You sons of heaven, you shall likewise attain unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment in that realm of *Sudarśanābhidhāna*, each having a distinct name yet sharing an identical lifespan."

Immediately, the trichiliocosm shook in six ways, and from the earth there spontaneously emerged immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of great jewel lotuses. Their petals were made of Jāmbūnada gold, their pedestals of celestial deep-blue lapis lazuli and mani-jewels, their filaments of musaragalva, and their stalks of vaidūrya. Within these lotuses, bodhisattvas appeared, sitting cross-legged with bodies adorned by the marks and signs of excellence; they paid respectful homage to the Buddha and offered various clouds and nets of necklaces to the World-Honored One, all saying:

"We each reside in different Buddha-worlds, and having heard from afar this *Acintya-bodhisattva-guṇa-sūtra*, we have come here to see the Buddha, the World-Honored One, to pay our respects and circumambulate him to the right, and also to see the good man Sāṭha and the great assembly."
He further said:
"World-Honored One!
There are inconceivable Buddha-fields with countless sentient beings who, having heard this sutra, shall all attain non-retrogression in the unsurpassed right path."
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
“Listen as I explain this meaning; With single-mindedness, do not let your thoughts wander.
The Tathāgata’s words are never false; The Tamer of Men has no other teaching.”
When Satyaka appeared in the world, more than billions of kalpas had passed;
he was named King of the Marks of True Intent. That kalpa was pure, free from the thorns of affliction, devoid of the thorn of lustful desire, and without many faults or transgressions.
Nor shall there be the thorn of delusion; that eon shall be free from thorns.
The world shall be known as "Well-Contemplated," adorned with various exquisite colors.
Gods and humans shall behold it with joy, for a Tamer of Men shall appear therein.
Wandering upon the high jeweled terrace, one shall behold universal adornment and purity.
Covered by nets of Jambū-river gold, with wondrous, soft sounds that delight the mind,
jeweled lion banners are erected, and precious golden nets are suspended.
With walls and parapets made of precious gems, there shall be celestial palaces,
and there shall be rivers, ponds, and wells— all adorned in every way.
Blue and white lotuses shall spread everywhere, and the water of eight flavors shall overflow in abundance.
In the central four continents, there is a place called Sight-Just-Appeared.
It is the city where the Sugata was born; he emerged from the Brahmin caste.
His mother’s name was Courageous, and his father was Brahmāpraśasta.
The Master said: "His fame was universal, like my son Rāhula.
His mother, the noble queen of that Sugata, was named Mahāmati, just as my own queen was Gopā. His wet nurse was named Mahāyaśas."
Now my wet nurse is named Gautamī; her attendant is named Anupamā.
She shall serve as the charioteer for the Tamer, providing for the Sugata just as I employ Chandaka.
The Horse-King among the Honored Bipeds shall be named Mahābala;
he shall carry the Sugata forth into homelessness, just as I, Kaṇṭhaka, did for him.
That Tathāgata’s place of awakening shall be named Dharmavīra.
Surrounded on all sides by eight billion hundred thousand trees,
the Honored One among Men sat beneath them; with a truly peerless mind,
he awakened to the unsurpassed path free from sorrow under the Bodhi tree.
There is no Māra, nor hosts of Māras, and ultimately there is no activity of Māra.
In the realm of the Sugata, there are no thorns; it is equal to existence and non-existence, like a Great Man (mahāpuruṣa).
In that world, there are sentient beings who perform meritorious deeds for humans and devas.
Adorned with flower garlands and accompanied by various musical performances, they went forth to the place where the World-Honored One was.
The Tamer of Men, knowing that the assembly had gathered and perceiving that their minds were ultimately pure,
was about to preach this King of Sutras, surrounded by billions of other sutras.
When this supreme sūtra was heard being preached by the Honored One Among Two-Legged Beings,
many billions of beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges attained non-retrogression from Buddha-wisdom;
they shall never again hear of the Lesser Vehicle, nor will there be any of the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle.
The bodhisattvas who are firm in wisdom exist in that Buddha-world.
In the first assembly of the Honored One among bipeds, there shall be as many as the sands of the Ganges—
bodhisattvas of great renown who are non-retrogressive in the ocean of merit.
In the second assembly, eighty nayutas [of beings] all attained the stage of being born only once more;
in the third assembly, sixty bimbaras [attained it], bringing great benefit to many virtuous bodhisattvas.
The lifespan of the Sugata shall fill sixty intermediate kalpas;
after the Tamer of Men has passed into extinction, the True Dharma will spread widely for eighty billion years, and the Dharma will remain for a nayuta of years.
The relics shall spread far and wide, and many sentient beings will be disciplined.
When the World-Honored One enters parinirvāṇa, he will bestow a prediction upon the Bodhisattva Mahālakṣaṇa:
"You shall become a charioteer of the world, named Mahāvyūha."
His adornments are likewise so, and his benefit for sentient beings is equal;
he shall become a World-Subduing Buddha on the unsurpassed, dustless path.
I know and see the unsurpassed, knowing that it shall take immeasurable kalpas.
How much more so when [the Buddha] is present before one, with all-knowledge unimpeded.
Believe my words as immeasurable; the Tathāgata’s words are not in vain.
Abide truthfully in my teaching and grasp the words I have spoken.
Having heard the Sugata’s teaching, the great assembly was filled with joy and courage;
they made a vow for that world, saying, "We shall be reborn there.
The World-Charioteer gave his prediction, saying they would be born in that stainless realm.
"You should awaken to the supreme path and extensively benefit all sentient beings who come to you.
When this king of sutras was spoken, the great earth shook in six ways;
from within the flowers, Bodhisattvas emerged, joining their palms in homage to the Tamer of Men.
“Excellent is the Awakened Man; he excellently teaches the Dharma without interruption.
Having heard the Buddha teach the Dharma, I have come from afar for the sake of the Dharma.

At that time, the entire great assembly was deeply satisfied; they rejoiced and leaped for joy, cherishing and upholding [the teaching]. They left behind only a single robe, offering all their other robes to the Buddha as an offering.
He spoke these words:

"The World-Honored One has appeared in the world and turned the Wheel of Dharma for a second time; having first turned the Wheel of Dharma at Vārāṇasī, he now once again turns the greatest Wheel of Dharma."
They all said:
“World-Honored One!
We pray that we may never be separated from such a jewel of the Dharma, nor ever be separated from this virtuous man.”

At that time, various celestial music resounded in the sky above, and great blue, yellow, red, and white lotuses rained down before the Buddha’s feet. Celestial garments whirled of their own accord in the void as the devas proclaimed these words:
“This virtuous man shall, in a future age, accomplish inconceivable merit—namely, whoever upholds this sutra, recites it with fluency, and explains it extensively for others.”
Having spoken these words, Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If these sons and daughters of good family write down this sutra, receive, uphold, read, and recite it until they have mastered it, and then extensively explain it to others, how much merit will they obtain?”
When he had asked this, the Buddha said: “Mañjuśrī!

Suppose there were a son of good family or a daughter of good family who, for the duration of one kalpa, were to reverently make offerings to, honor, respect, and prostrate before all the Buddhas throughout the trichiliocosm—including all sentient beings, whether with form or without form, with perception or without perception, and the entire realm of sentient beings, of whom only a Buddha knows the full extent—causing those who have not yet attained a human body to attain it, and having them achieve unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment; and suppose they were to provide them with every comfort. Mañjuśrī! If another son of good family or daughter of good family were to hear even a single verse of this *Sūtra of the Lotus of the True Dharma* and rejoice in it, their merit would exceed that of the former.”
Mañjuśrī! What do you think? Would these sons or daughters of good family obtain much merit by reason of this cause and condition?
Mañjuśrī replied: “Very many, World-Honored One! Very many, Sugata!”
"There is nothing that can be numbered and nothing that can be measured. The Buddha said, "Mañjuśrī!"

If these sons or daughters of good family write down, receive, uphold, read, recite, and master this [teaching], and explain it extensively for others, their merit will be far greater than that of the sons or daughters of good family who make offerings to the Buddhas.
Mañjuśrī said: “World-Honored One! It is unprecedented that the World-Honored One, for the benefit of all the world, has preached this sutra.”
“World-Honored One!
For how long shall this sutra circulate within Jambudvīpa?
The Buddha said:
“Mañjuśrī! After my parinirvāṇa, my śarīra shall be widely distributed. At that time, eight kings shall divide my śarīra using jeweled caskets into eight portions;

having done so, each shall construct a great stūpa within their own kingdom. King Ajātaśatru shall take the eighth portion of my śarīra, place it in a precious incense casket, and bury it by excavating the earth outside the city of Rājagṛha. He shall enshrine various kinds of exquisite and diverse fragrances, erect various banners, pennants, and jeweled canopies, scatter various precious flowers, and light lamps that burn for a hundred years, thereby concealing the śarīra casket.”
"Wait for King Aśoka; he shall inscribe this King of Sūtras upon golden leaves and conceal them. Mañjuśrī! One hundred years after my parinirvāṇa, there shall be a King Aśoka.

This king shall arise from the Malla kṣatriya clan and rule over Jambudvīpa. He shall attain sovereign power as a Cakravartin king dwelling in the four continents. At that time, that king will cultivate mindfulness of my teachings and attain a pure mind within the Buddha-dharma."

"At that time, there was a bhikṣu named Indrasama who had attained great supernormal powers and possessed great majestic virtue. He upheld the *Saddharma* and the *Vaipulya Sūtras*; born of royal lineage, he had renounced the world and frequently entered and exited the palace of the Great King Aśoka."

Mañjuśrī! King Aśoka, in order to widely disseminate my relics, was accompanied by a vast retinue of nobles and dignitaries; adorned with the majesty and power of a great king, he took various flower garlands, powdered incense, unguents, and diverse musical instruments, and arrived at the city of Rājagṛha to perform a grand offering. He excavated the ground to retrieve the relic casket and, for seven days, performed various offerings. Having made such a great offering with all kinds of flowers, all garlands, all powdered incense, all unguents, and all musical instruments—
Thereafter, in various places where many people dwell, eighty-four thousand great stupas were erected in a single day and at one time.

At that time, after the Dharma Master Indraśama had taken this sutra from the precious casket and established it in a northern region where many people reside, this sutra was not known by many people, nor understood by many people, nor received by many people; only a few people received, upheld, read, and recited this sutra.
Mañjuśrī! This sutra is mostly hidden away in chests and boxes. Why is this?
Because no one receives it and because they are not true vessels, Mañjuśrī!

You should know that this sutra is difficult to understand and difficult to believe; it is difficult to fathom its depths. It is not something that ordinary people can believe and accept, nor is it something that those of inferior capacity can read or enter.
Mañjuśrī! In the final fifty years, if there should be anyone who hears this sutra and believes, understands, and reveres it, Mañjuśrī!
One should not harbor doubts; you should know that such persons have made offerings to many Buddhas, have practiced well in this Mahāyāna sūtra, and are true vessels for it.

If there are those who copy, uphold, read, recite, and master this sūtra, these sentient beings should know for themselves: "We have already seen as many Tathāgatas as the sands of the Ganges, whom we have served, honored, circumambulated, and prostrated to; we have also seen me here in this grove preaching this sūtra, as well as the great assembly."
At that time, the Buddha told Ānanda:
“Receive this sutra, read it, recite it, and master it thoroughly. You must be careful not to preach this scripture before those of low station, for they do not know their own spiritual capacities.”
Why is this? Ānanda! These are the merits of the Tathāgata;
these are the secret places of the Tathāgata; these are the teachings spoken by the Tathāgata, which are purely and without admixture the Dharma.
"This is the seal of the Tathāgata; this is the firm dharma of the Tathāgata; this is the supreme wealth of the Tathāgata. Ānanda!
You should hold it fast and not give it recklessly to others, except for my eldest son who upholds my treasury of Dharma and protects my treasury of Dharma—grant it to such persons as these."
Ānanda said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One, I have already received and upheld this sutra.”
"What is the name of this sutra?
How should it be upheld?
The Buddha said:

“Ānanda! This sutra is titled ‘The Sutra on the Supernatural Transformations and the Realm of Skillful Means in the Bodhisattva’s Practice’; it is also titled ‘The Secret Abode of the Tathāgata,’ also titled ‘The Tathāgata’s Teaching of Pure and Unadulterated Dharmas,’ also titled ‘The Tathāgata’s Expounding of the Single Vehicle,’ also titled ‘The Questions of Mañjuśrī,’ also titled ‘The Prophecy for Satyaka,’ and also titled ‘The Chapter on Satyaka. You should uphold it thus.”
When the Tathāgata preached this Dharma-sūtra, thirty nayutas of sentient beings who had never before resolved to attain the unsurpassed path all now gave rise to that resolve;
sixty thousand bodhisattvas attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti);
and immeasurable sentient beings became fixed in the path of supreme, perfect, and true enlightenment.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the Venerable Ānanda was joyful and satisfied;

Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, all the bodhisattvas, the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās, as well as Śakra, Brahmā, the world-protecting devas, and the people of the world, having heard what the Buddha spoke, were filled with joy and accepted it with faith.
